You’ve solved a few hundred Kakuro grids, and one evening you decide to make one. Graph paper, a pencil, an hour. You shade some black squares, write digits in the white ones, add up the sums, and hand the finished puzzle to a friend. Ten minutes later they slide it back across the table. The four cells at the bottom of the grid work as 9 8 over 8 9, and they also work as 8 9 over 9 8. Every clue checks out both ways.

Your puzzle has two answers, and nothing on the page tells you what went wrong.

Solving a Kakuro means following a path someone else built. Making one means building that path yourself and then proving there’s no second way through. That second part is where most first attempts fail, and it’s the part generator tools never explain. This series builds one 7x7 grid from blank paper to finished puzzle, and this article walks the whole route once: the layout, a first fill that fails, a one-digit repair, a difficulty grade, and a harder version of the same grid.

The Anatomy of a Kakuro Grid

The Layout Rules

A Kakuro grid has two kinds of squares. White cells take a single digit from 1 to 9. Black cells hold the clues, or nothing at all. A clue cell is split by a diagonal: the number above the line is the sum of the white cells to its right, and the number below is the sum of the white cells beneath it.

Each unbroken line of white cells is a run, and four rules govern the layout:

  • Runs are 2 to 9 cells long. A one-cell run would print the answer in the clue. Ten cells can’t work, because digits can’t repeat within a run and there are only nine of them.
  • Every white cell sits in one across run and one down run. A cell with only one direction has nothing to cross-check it.
  • All white cells connect. No islands, no corners touching diagonally and calling it a bridge.
  • No digit repeats within a run. This is the rule that makes unique solutions possible at all.

Here’s the layout this whole series uses. Row 0 and column 0 form the clue border; the playable interior is 6x6.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |#######|       |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|       |       |#######|       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

It has 24 white cells and 16 runs: six of 2 cells, four of 3 and six of 4. Designing a Kakuro Grid builds it one black cell at a time.

Symmetry

Turn the layout upside down and the black-and-white pattern looks the same. That’s 180° rotational symmetry, and while it isn’t one of Kakuro’s rules (Nikoli lists exactly three, none about layout), it’s the convention for hand-made grids.

Measure it on the interior, not the border. The clue border runs along the top and left, so a half-turn would move it to the bottom and right, and no grid would ever pass. In the series grid, interior cell (r, c) pairs with (7 − r, 7 − c): the black cell at r3c3 pairs with r4c4, and r1c5 pairs with r6c2.

Two Ways to Build: Fill-First vs. Clue-First

Fill-First

Lay out the grid, write a digit in every white cell without repeating within a run, then add up each run to get its clue. It’s fast, and it’s how most computer generators work. The catch is that a valid fill proves one solution exists. It says nothing about a second one, and most fills have several. The series grid was built this way, and its first fill failed exactly like the one in the opening.

Clue-First

Pick a clue, work out what it forces, then pick the next clue to build on that. You solve the puzzle in your head as you write it, which means you control where the solver starts and what each step demands.

Here’s how a clue-first start looks in the series grid’s bottom-right corner. Put a 6 on the three-cell down run along the right edge. Six in three cells can only be {1, 2, 3}. Put a 27 on the bottom across run. Twenty-seven in four cells is {3, 7, 8, 9}, {4, 6, 8, 9} or {5, 6, 7, 9}. The corner cell belongs to both runs, and the only digit both allow is 3. That’s your first forced move. The next clue you choose should build on that 3.

Watch which clues you cross. A 3 in two cells is {1, 2}; a 17 in two cells is {8, 9}. Cross them and the shared cell has no possible digit. Good crossings share exactly one digit: 17 against 16 ({7, 9}) forces 9, and 3 against 4 ({1, 3}) forces 1.

Exactly One Solution

Back to the opening. Here’s the series grid’s first fill, with the four trouble cells in brackets:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |   6   |   3   |   2   |   1   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   9   |   6   |   8   |   4   | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 24\8  |   3   |   5   |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |   1   |   7   | 17\8  |   6   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \21 |  [9]  |  [8]  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |  [8]  |  [9]  |   7   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Swap the bracketed cells to 8 9 over 9 8 and every run still holds exactly the same digits, just in a different order. The 21 across still holds {9, 8, 3, 1}. The 24 down still holds {7, 8, 9}. That’s a swap, sometimes called a deadly pattern, and no clue can catch it because no clue cares about order.

Notice what runs through those four cells: a 24 in three cells and a 17 in two. Both are magic blocks, clues with only one possible digit set. They don’t help. A magic block fixes which digits a run uses, not where they go.

The fix is to change a digit. Change r5c3 from 9 to 4 and recalculate the two clues through it: the row-5 across becomes 16 and the column-3 down becomes 19. Now the only way to shift those four cells would put a second 3 in row 5, and the no-repeat rule kills it.

To prove the repaired grid has one solution, solve it using only forced moves. If every placement is the only option at the moment you make it, there’s no room for a second answer. How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution covers swaps, longer loops and the repair options in full.

Setting the Difficulty

A big grid isn’t a hard grid. Difficulty is the hardest technique the solver must use, and you choose it when you choose the digits. This series grades on four tiers:

  1. Magic blocks. Read the digits almost straight off the clue.
  2. Intersections. Compare the possible digits of two crossing runs.
  3. Region counts. Add a block’s across clues, add its down clues, and the difference is a cell only one direction covers. (No 45 needed; see Mastering the 45 Rule.)
  4. Parity and chains. Odd/even counting and short if-then chains.

The repaired series grid, with three magic blocks, solves on tiers 1 and 2 alone, so it grades Medium. A second version keeps the same layout, changes every digit, and drops to one magic block. Seven cells fall, then everything stalls until you count the top-left block across against down. That’s a Hard grid built on the same skeleton. How to Set Kakuro Difficulty builds it step by step.

Practical Example: The Series Grid, Start to Finish

Here’s the full route the series grid took, in the order you’d follow on your own grid.

  1. Lay out a symmetric skeleton. Place black cells in pairs, (r, c) and (7 − r, 7 − c), and check for one-cell runs and disconnected pockets after every pair.
  2. Fill the digits. Write 1–9 in every white cell with no repeats within a run, then add up all 16 runs to get the clues. This is the draft above.
  3. Test-solve, looking for a second answer. Check every 2x2 block of white cells for the A B over B A pattern. The series layout has eight such blocks; the swap sits in the one at r5c3–r6c4.
  4. Repair. Change r5c3 from 9 to 4. Recalculate the row-5 across (21 becomes 16) and the column-3 down (24 becomes 19).
  5. Prove it. Solve the new grid with forced moves only. The first one is r6c6 = 3, the 6-down against 27-across crossing from earlier. Every other cell follows without a guess.
  6. Grade it. The hardest step was an intersection, so it’s Medium.

Steps 3 and 4 form a loop. You keep testing and repairing until no second answer turns up:

Here’s the finished puzzle:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |       |       |       |       | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |       |       | 19\8  |       |       |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |       |       | 17\8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

One solution, three magic blocks, every move forced. You can print it along with the Hard version and solve both on paper.

A Brief History: From Cross Sums to Kakuro

The puzzle reached most English-speaking solvers as Cross Sums, a name credited to Jacob E. Funk, a Canadian working for Dell Magazines. Sources disagree on the year: some say 1950, while Wikipedia says 1966. In Japan, Nikoli introduced the puzzle in issue 11 of its magazine as kasan kurosu, “addition cross,” and the name was shortened to Kakuro. It stayed the most popular logic puzzle in Japanese print until Sudoku took the top spot in 1992.

Nikoli’s rules for it still fit in three lines: digits 1 through 9, no zeros; each clue is the sum of the cells to its right or below; no digit repeats within a run. Everything in this series comes down to arranging those three rules so a solver can find their way through, and only one way.

Best Practices for Constructors

Do:

  • ✓ Solve your own puzzle from scratch, with forced moves only, before anyone else sees it.
  • ✓ Keep the interior symmetric if you plan to publish.
  • ✓ Give the solver at least one clear place to start.
  • ✓ Check every 2x2 block of white cells for a swap before you calculate clues.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Assume a valid fill has only one solution.
  • ✗ Try to fix a swap by turning one of its runs into a magic block. It won’t work.
  • ✗ Use guessing as a difficulty feature. Hard should mean a harder deduction, not a coin flip.

Troubleshooting Common Construction Mistakes

Four cells in a rectangle can trade digits. The rectangle holds A B over B A, so every run through it keeps the same digits. Change one of the four digits and recalculate its two clues, or move a black cell to split one of the runs. To catch it earlier, look for matching digits on opposite corners of every 2x2 white block before you add anything up.

The puzzle has no solution. Usually a clue was added up wrong or a digit repeats within a run. Recheck each clue against the filled grid, one run at a time. To prevent it, always calculate clues from the finished fill rather than writing them from memory.

A crossing has no possible digit. Two crossing clues share no digit, like a 3 in two cells across a 17 in two cells. Change one of the clues (and the digits beneath it) so the two sets overlap.

Where to Go Next

Making a Kakuro comes down to designing a solving path and then proving it’s the only one. The layout decides where the solver can start and where swaps can hide. Pure swaps slip past every clue, so you fix them with digits or black cells. And difficulty is the hardest step you force, not the size of the grid.

Print the series layout and try your own fill, or work through the finished series puzzles. If you’d like to see Kakuro grids doing more than sitting on a page, every door in Escape the Crimson Gala opens with one.

content:
The Kakuro book said “Expert.” You believed it for the first ten minutes, while the corners filled in nicely. Now you’re looking at a block in the middle of the grid where every clue has five ways to be right, your pencil marks are three deep, and the eraser has worn a soft gray patch into the paper. You’re one bad decision away from picking a digit and hoping.

You don’t need to be better at arithmetic. Expert Kakuro grids are built to resist the tools that got you through the medium ones, so you need a few more tools. There are four of them, and each one picks up where the last runs out: magic blocks give you a starting point, intersections turn candidates into digits, the 45 rule opens blocks with no starting point, and parity and forcing chains settle the corners where everything else stalls.

Mastering Magic Blocks (Unique Sums)

Small Magic Blocks

Kakuro has two rules: digits 1 through 9, and no repeats inside an entry (the run of white cells a clue covers). Near the ends of the number range, those two rules leave only one possible set of digits for a clue. Conceptis Puzzles calls those clues magic blocks, and they’re the first thing to look for on any grid.

The small ones show up in almost every puzzle:

Cells Low High
2 3 {1,2} · 4 {1,3} 16 {7,9} · 17 {8,9}
3 6 {1,2,3} · 7 {1,2,4} 23 {6,8,9} · 24 {7,8,9}

Memorizing these isn’t about saving three seconds of addition. It changes what you see. Once “17 in two cells” reads as “8 and 9”, you stop calculating and start noticing that the 17 crosses a 16, and that the two share only the digit 9. That cell is solved before you’ve picked up the pencil.

Large Magic Blocks

Four and five cells have their own extremes: 10 {1,2,3,4}, 11 {1,2,3,5}, 29 {5,7,8,9}, and 30 {6,7,8,9} in four cells, and 15, 16, 34, and 35 in five. These rarely place a digit directly, but they cap or floor every entry that crosses them. Every cell of a 10 in four cells is 4 or lower, which wipes out the high half of any crossing pair.

One trap catches people here: “10 in four cells” is not 1 + 1 + 4 + 4 or 2 + 2 + 3 + 3. Repeats are illegal, which is exactly why 10 has only one answer.

The full table, plus a walkthrough of finding every entry point on a blank grid, is in Essential Magic Blocks.

The Power of the 45 Rule

Basic Application

1 + 2 + … + 9 = 45. Killer Sudoku players use that fact constantly, because every box must hold each digit once. Kakuro has no such boxes. An open 3×3 block can legally hold 1, 2, 3 in every row and column and total 18. Only a nine-cell entry is guaranteed to total 45.

The rule still earns its place in two ways.

Long entries are short entries inside out. An eight-cell entry skips exactly one digit, and that digit is 45 minus the clue: 38 in eight cells is missing 7. A 41 in seven cells is missing two digits that total 4, which can only be {1, 3}.

Innies and outies. Pick a region. Add the across clues of every entry that lies wholly inside it, then add the down clues the same way. If one direction covers one extra cell, the difference between the two totals is that cell. An outie sits just outside the region, caught by an entry that pokes out. An innie sits inside, missed by an entry that leaves.

Advanced Block Math

Regions don’t have to be rectangles. Any shape works as long as each entry you count is completely inside it. If the totals differ by two cells instead of one, you haven’t failed: you’ve made a new two-cell clue, and if it lands on 3, 4, 16, or 17, it’s a magic block.

The full method, including a grid where the count is the only way in, is in Mastering the 45 Rule.

Utilizing Intersection Logic

Cross-Referencing Extremes

Every entry has a ceiling and a floor. The highest digit a 14 in four cells can hold is 14 − (1 + 2 + 3) = 8. Cross that 14 with a 17 in two cells {8, 9}, and the shared cell can’t be 9, so it’s 8. One crossing decided the cell and the 17’s other cell, and it settled the 14 as {1, 2, 3, 8}.

Push the extremes too far apart and the crossing becomes impossible. A 16 {7, 9} can’t share a cell with a 10 in four cells {1, 2, 3, 4}. You’ll never see that in a valid puzzle. If you think you do, recount the cells.

Forcing Digits

Most crossings narrow instead of solving. A 17 across over a 24 down {7, 8, 9} leaves 8 or 9 in the corner. A second crossing finishes the job: if the 17’s other cell sits on a 16 down {7, 9}, that cell must be 9, and the corner must be 8.

The habit that makes this fast is simple: read the crossing clue before writing any candidates. Intersection Logic has a cheat sheet of the crossings that force digits outright.

Eliminating Guesswork with Parity

Parity Rules

When a corner stalls with two fills that both seem to work, the temptation is bifurcation: pick one and see if it breaks. Don’t. A wrong guess usually fails ten moves later, far from where you made it.

Parity is the first tool for a stuck corner. An odd clue in two cells means one odd digit and one even digit. An even clue means both odd or both even. A 4 {1, 3} and a 16 {7, 9} are made entirely of odd digits, so if a cell in one of them crosses an odd two-cell clue, the other cell of that clue must be even.

The second tool is the forcing chain: assume a candidate, follow only forced moves, and look for a “ghost” duplicate, a digit the chain would place twice in the same entry. Three or four forced links that end in a collision prove the candidate wrong. You never write the assumption down. Eliminating the Guesswork walks through a corner that looks like two valid solutions until a chain finds the ghost.

Practical Example: Solving an Expert Grid Section

Here’s a four-row section with an irregular edge. Clue cells read down\across: 17\12 holds a down 17 and an across 12.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 10\   | 16\   | 15\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \13 |       |       |       |#######| 12\   | 15\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |       |       |       | 17\12 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \24 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \15 |       |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 1: Magic blocks. Scan for the short list. The 16 down is two cells, so {7, 9}. The 17 down is two cells, so {8, 9}. Everything else has at least two possible sets. Pencil those two blocks in and look for crossings. There aren’t any that settle a digit, which is why this section is rated expert.

Step 2: The 45 rule. The top-left block is a closed 2×3 region. Its across clues cover it exactly: 13 + 21 = 34. Its down clues cover it plus one cell, because the 15 down runs one cell past the block: 10 + 16 + 15 = 41.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 10\   | 16\   | 15\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \13 |   ·   |  7 9  |   ·   |#######| 12\   | 15\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |   ·   |  7 9  |   ·   | 17\12 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \24 | OUTIE |  8 9  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \15 |  8 9  |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The outie is 41 − 34 = 7.

Step 3: Intersections and a ghost on the left. With 7 at its bottom, the 15 down needs 8 from its top two cells: {2, 6} or {3, 5}, since {1, 7} would repeat the 7.

Now test the 21 across. Its sets are {4, 8, 9}, {5, 7, 9}, and {6, 7, 8}. Its right-hand cell has to come from {2, 3, 5, 6}, which rules out {4, 8, 9}. Try {6, 7, 8}: the right cell is 6, the middle is 7 (the 16 down allows only 7 or 9), and the left cell is 8. Follow the chain. The 10 down puts 2 above the 8. The 15 down puts 2 above the 6. That’s two 2s in the 13 across, a ghost duplicate, so {6, 7, 8} is out.

That leaves {5, 7, 9}. The right cell is 5, so the cell above it is 3. The 10 down is even, and its bottom cell is 7 or 9, both odd, so its top cell is odd as well: 1 or 3. 3 is already in the 13 across, so it’s 1, and the cell below is 9. The 16 down finishes as 9 over 7. Check the 13 across: 1 + 9 + 3 = 13.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 10\   | 16\   | 15\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \13 |   1   |   9   |   3   |#######| 12\   | 15\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |   9   |   7   |   5   | 17\12 |       | 7 8 9 |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \24 |   7   |  8 9  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \15 |  8 9  |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 4: Intersections on the right. The top-right cell sits in a 12 across ({3, 9}, {4, 8}, {5, 7}) and a 15 down ({6, 9}, {7, 8}). The digits both allow are 7, 8, and 9. The cell below it is 15 minus that, so 8, 7, or 6. The 24 across already has a 7, so it’s 8 or 6.

If it were 8, the 17 down cell in the same row would have to be 9 (the 8 is taken), and the 24 across would need 24 − 7 − 9 − 8 = 0 from its one remaining cell. Impossible. So it’s 6, the cell above is 9, and the 12 across starts with 3. The 24 across now needs 11 from its middle two cells, with the left one 8 or 9. The right one would be 3 or 2, and 3 is already in that column, so it’s 2 and the left is 9. The 17 down finishes with 8, and the 15 across needs 7 beside it. Check the 12 down: 3 + 2 + 7 = 12.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 10\   | 16\   | 15\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \13 |   1   |   9   |   3   |#######| 12\   | 15\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |   9   |   7   |   5   | 17\12 |   3   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \24 |   7   |   9   |   2   |   6   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \15 |   8   |   7   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Every technique made an appearance. The magic blocks gave you candidates. The 45 rule gave you the first digit. Intersections and one short ghost chain did the rest. Not one guess.

Best Practices and Tips

Do:

  • ✓ Memorize the 2-, 3-, and 4-cell extremes.
  • ✓ Keep pencil marks small and in the same spot in each cell, so you can read them at a glance.
  • ✓ Check the crossing clue before writing candidates in any cell.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Guess. If you’re tempted, look for a ghost duplicate first.
  • ✗ Forget that digits can’t repeat inside an entry. It’s the rule that makes every technique here work.
  • ✗ Ignore large open blocks. That’s exactly where the 45 rule pays off.

Speed tips:

  • Scan the whole grid for 3, 4, 16, and 17 before touching anything else.
  • Work from the edges in. Corners and short entries constrain the most.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

Two possibilities remain for the last two cells.

  • Cause: You missed a duplicate in a crossing entry, or a clue elsewhere that tells the two fills apart.
  • Fix: Fill each option in your head and check every entry it touches, including cells just outside the pair.
  • Prevention: Check both crossing entries every time you lock in a digit.

The sums don’t add up at the end.

  • Cause: An arithmetic slip early on, or a repeated digit inside one entry.
  • Fix: Go back to the last digit you’re certain of and redo the steps after it. If the error is too old to find, start the grid fresh. Painful, but faster than unpicking a tangle.

The 45-rule count gives a digit above 9.

  • Cause: An entry in your count pokes out of the region, or you assumed a block sums to 45.
  • Fix: Count only entries completely inside the region, and compare across with down. Don’t compare against 45.

Conclusion

Key takeaways:

  1. Magic blocks are your entry points.
  2. Intersections turn those entry points into placed digits.
  3. The 45 rule opens large blocks with no magic blocks in them.
  4. Parity and short forcing chains settle the corners where everything else stalls, with no guessing.
  5. Recognizing patterns is faster than recalculating combinations.

Next steps: Practice spotting magic blocks on an easy grid until you stop reaching for the table. Then try innies and outies on a Killer Sudoku, where the regions are handed to you, before hunting for them in Kakuro.

title: The Ultimate Guide to Advanced Kakuro Tactics

content:
Your first Kakuro grid looks like a crossword someone forgot to finish. Black squares are slashed with diagonal lines, small numbers sit in their corners, and rows of empty white boxes wait for you. You pick the first clue you see, a 15 across three cells, and start trying combinations. 9, 5, 1? 8, 4, 3? 7, 6, 2? Ten minutes later your eraser has worn a shiny patch into the paper and you haven’t committed a single digit.

You haven’t done anything wrong. You’ve just started in the wrong place. That 15 has eight different valid combinations, and nothing on the board tells you which one is right yet. Somewhere else on that same grid sits a clue with exactly one possible answer, and that’s where every solve should begin.

Kakuro rewards a specific order of operations: read the grid correctly, find the clues that can only be solved one way, then use the places where clues cross to pin down exact digits. None of it requires guessing. All of it requires knowing where to look first.

The Anatomy of a Kakuro Grid

Kakuro has been around longer than most people expect. Dell published it as Cross Sums in 1950, and Nikoli brought it to Japan in 1980 under the name Kasan Kurosu, which roughly means “addition cross.” Nikoli shortened that to Kakuro in 1986, and the name stuck. The rules have barely changed since.

Reading the Clues

Nikoli’s official rules boil down to three lines:

  1. Put a digit from 1 to 9 in every white cell. No zeros, no two-digit numbers.
  2. A number in a cell split by a diagonal line gives the sum of the consecutive white cells to its right or below it.
  3. No digit may appear more than once in the same run of consecutive cells.

The black cells hold the clues. When a black cell is split diagonally, the number in the top-right triangle belongs to the white cells running to the right. The number in the bottom-left triangle belongs to the white cells running down. A black cell can carry one clue, both, or none.

Each unbroken run of white cells is called an entry. An entry starts right after its clue cell and stops at the next black cell or the edge of the grid. Entries are always at least two cells long and never more than nine. A nine-cell entry has to use every digit from 1 to 9 once, so its clue is always 45.

In the diagrams throughout this series, a clue cell is written as down\across. So 3\ is a down clue of 3, \4 is an across clue of 4, and 24\16 carries both: 24 for the entry below it, 16 for the entry to its right.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

This small corner has four entries. The \4 cell says the two white cells to its right add up to 4. The 3\ cell says the two white cells below it add up to 3. The top-left white cell belongs to both of those entries at once, and that overlap is where the solving happens.

The no-repeat rule applies only within an entry. A clue of 4 across two cells can’t be 2 + 2. But the same row can hold two 4s if a black cell splits them into separate entries. The rule doesn’t care about rows or columns the way Sudoku does. It cares only about the entry.

The “No Trial and Error” Rule

Every published Kakuro has exactly one solution, and you can reach it by deduction alone. Guessing feels faster, but it isn’t.

Take the corner above. The top-left white cell sits in the across 4, which has to be 1 + 3. Suppose you guess it’s the 3. The across entry looks fine: 3 + 1 = 4. Now check the down entry. The down 3 needs two cells that add to 3, and you’ve already spent 3 on the first one. The second cell would have to be 0, which doesn’t exist.

In a 2x2 corner, the contradiction shows up in one move. On a 10x10 grid, a bad guess can survive for twenty moves before something finally fails to add up, and by then you can’t tell which digit started it.

Instead of committing, write pencil marks: small candidate digits in the corner of a cell. They cost nothing to erase and they keep every option visible until the logic narrows it to one.

The Magic of Unique Sums

Some clues can only be made one way. These unique sums are the foothold on any grid, and you should find all of them before you write a single final digit.

The Extremes: Highs and Lows

The smallest two-cell sum is 3, and the largest is 17. At both ends, the options run out fast.

  • 3 in two cells: 1 + 2. Nothing else works.
  • 4 in two cells: 1 + 3. The only other option, 2 + 2, repeats a digit.
  • 16 in two cells: 7 + 9. The only other option, 8 + 8, repeats a digit.
  • 17 in two cells: 8 + 9. Nothing else works.

Compare that to a 5 in two cells, which could be 1 + 4 or 2 + 3. One extra point of sum doubles your options. A 10 in two cells has four options (1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6), so it tells you almost nothing on its own.

When you spot a 3, 4, 16, or 17 over a two-cell entry, you know both digits immediately. You don’t know their order yet, but you know the set, and that’s enough to pencil them in.

Extended Unique Sums

The same squeeze happens on longer entries. Every entry length from two to seven cells has exactly four unique sums, two at the low end and two at the high end. Conceptis Puzzles calls these “magic blocks.”

Entry length Unique low sums Unique high sums
2 cells 3 = {1,2} · 4 = {1,3} 16 = {7,9} · 17 = {8,9}
3 cells 6 = {1,2,3} · 7 = {1,2,4} 23 = {6,8,9} · 24 = {7,8,9}
4 cells 10 = {1,2,3,4} · 11 = {1,2,3,5} 29 = {5,7,8,9} · 30 = {6,7,8,9}
5 cells 15 = {1,2,3,4,5} · 16 = {1,2,3,4,6} 34 = {4,6,7,8,9} · 35 = {5,6,7,8,9}

There’s a shortcut for remembering the high side. Swap each digit in a low set for 10 minus that digit, and you get its high twin. {1,2} becomes {9,8}, so 3 pairs with 17. {1,2,4} becomes {9,8,6}, so 7 pairs with 23.

To scan a new grid, ignore everything in the middle range on your first pass. Look for small numbers over short entries and big numbers over short entries. Pencil in the digit sets as you find them. Small beginner grids are packed with these. The 6x6 practice grid in Kakuro Unique Sums has nine of them, and you can find every one before you’ve done any real thinking.

Cross-Referencing: Your Most Powerful Tool

Unique sums tell you which digits. Cross-referencing tells you where.

Finding the Intersection

Every white cell belongs to exactly two entries: one across and one down. Whatever digit goes in that cell has to work for both clues. If the across entry allows {1,3} and the down entry allows {1,2}, the shared cell can only hold a digit that appears in both sets. That’s 1.

This is the whole engine of Kakuro. Each clue on its own is a small arithmetic problem with several answers. Two clues crossing at one cell shrink each other’s options, often down to a single digit.

The “Forced Digit” Deduction

Once you place a digit, every entry it touches gets smaller. Say a 10 runs across three cells and you’ve just placed a 1 in one of them. The remaining two cells now need to sum to 9, and they can’t use 1. That leaves {2,7}, {3,6}, or {4,5}. You’ve turned a three-cell problem into a two-cell problem.

Sometimes that shrinking leaves exactly one option. When an entry has one empty cell left, its value is simply the clue minus everything already placed. That’s a forced digit: no choice involved, just subtraction. Placing it then shrinks the other entry that cell belongs to, and the chain continues.

Practical Example: Solving a Corner

Back to the corner from earlier. This time, solve it.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

Step 1: Find the unique sums. The across 4 over two cells must be {1,3}. The down 3 over two cells must be {1,2}. Pencil them in.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |  1 3  |  1 3  |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \8  |  1 2  |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

Step 2: Look at the intersection. The top-left white cell carries {1,3} from the across clue and {1,2} from the down clue. The only digit in both sets is 1.

Step 3: Write the digit. The top-left cell is 1.

Step 4: Finish both entries. The across 4 needs 4 − 1 = 3 in the next cell. The down 3 needs 3 − 1 = 2 in the cell below.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   1   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \8  |   2   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

Step 5: Take the forced digit. The bottom-right cell is the last empty cell in two entries. The across 8 needs 8 − 2 = 6. The down 9 needs 9 − 3 = 6. Both clues agree, which is your confirmation.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   1   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \8  |   2   |   6   |
+-------+-------+-------+

Four cells, zero guesses. Every digit came from either a unique sum, an intersection, or subtraction. That same loop solves full grids:

The Kakuro Solving Loop

Visualizing the core deduction cycle:

graph TD
    A[1. Scan for Unique Sums] --> B[Pencil in Digit Sets]
    B --> C{2. Intersect Entries}
    C -->|Single Shared Candidate| D[3. Place Digit]
    C -->|Multiple Candidates| C
    D --> E[Subtract Digit from Both Clues]
    E --> F[4. Update Pencil Marks]
    F --> G{Are Clues Fulfilled?}
    G -->|No| C
    G -->|Yes| H[Check Addition]
    H --> C
  1. Scan for unique sums and pencil in their digit sets.
  2. Intersect crossing entries to find cells with a single shared candidate.
  3. Place the digit and subtract it from both entries it belongs to.
  4. Update pencil marks in both entries, then look for the next forced digit.

Do’s and Don’ts

Do:

  • ✓ Scan the entire grid for unique sums before writing anything in pen.
  • ✓ Use small pencil marks for candidates and erase them as soon as they’re ruled out.
  • ✓ Check the addition in both directions every time you complete an entry.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Place a digit because it fits one clue. It has to fit both.
  • ✗ Repeat a digit inside an entry, even in a long one where the first cell is far away.
  • ✗ Ignore the crossing point of two long entries. Late in a solve, those often hold the forced digit you need.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

“I’m stuck and can’t find the next move.” Usually you’ve missed an intersection, or you placed a digit and didn’t update the pencil marks around it. Re-scan the grid for entries that now have fewer empty cells. A five-cell 25 with three digits placed is now a two-cell problem, and it might be a unique sum. To prevent this, trace both the across and down entries every time you write a permanent digit.

“My last cell doesn’t add up.” Somewhere upstream there’s an arithmetic slip or a repeated digit. Work backward through the entry that failed, then through each crossing entry, checking sums and duplicates as you go. Most broken grids trace back to a single wrong digit. To prevent this, re-add every entry in both directions as you finish it, not at the end.

Conclusion

Kakuro looks like a math test, but the arithmetic is the easy part. The skill is knowing where to start and refusing to guess.

Key takeaways:

  1. Kakuro rewards logic, not trial and error. Every digit can be proven.
  2. Unique sums such as 3, 4, 16, and 17 in two cells are your starting anchors.
  3. Every white cell has to satisfy both its across clue and its down clue.
  4. Cross-referencing two crossing entries reveals forced digits, and each placed digit shrinks the problem further.

Next steps: Print a beginner grid, run a unique-sum scan before you write anything in pen, and work outward from the corners. When the 2-cell sums feel automatic, start memorizing the 3-cell and 4-cell sets from the table above.

You have nine clues and a dead lord. Clue one says Dr. Pryce wasn’t seen at 9:45. Fine. Clue three says he wasn’t seen at 9:30 either. Two ✕s later, the doctor’s row in the Time block has only two squares left, and clue eight is already whispering about which one. That narrowing is the reason people have been doing these on train rides for sixty years.

This one is a classic logic grid: every guest was in exactly one room, holding exactly one object, at exactly one time. Nothing is shared and nothing is left over. The clues never lie, and they’re enough to pin down every pairing without a single guess. The generator that built this puzzle rejected every clue set that needed trial and error.

The case

Loading puzzle...

How the grid works

Each small square crosses one item against another, so the square where Colonel Ashby meets Library asks “was the Colonel in the Library?”

  • Tap once for ✕ when a clue rules a pairing out.
  • Tap twice for ● when you’re certain two things go together. The rest of that row and column inside the same block fills with faded ✕s for you, because each guest can only be in one room.
  • Tap a third time to clear the square. Any faded ✕s that only existed because of it disappear too.

Tap a clue to strike it through once you’ve squeezed everything out of it. Your marks save on this device automatically, so you can close the tab mid-case and come back later.

Stuck?

Try these before you reach for the hint button. Each one is a technique, not a spoiler.

  1. Work the “one of these two” clues first. “Of A and B, one was X and the other was Y” rules out four pairings and links two guests at once. They do more work than any other clue type here.
  2. Read the time clues as a ladder. “Exactly fifteen minutes before” means neither guest can be at the ends of the ladder in the wrong direction. The guest seen earlier can’t be at 9:45, and the later one can’t be at 9:00.
  3. Cross-reference blocks. Once you know Lady Vane held a certain object, everything you know about that object’s time or room now applies to her too. Copy those marks across.

The Check Solution button outlines any mark that contradicts the evidence, including faded ✕s caused by a wrong ●. It counts as a mistake on your final score, so use it when you’re sure, not when you’re curious.

content:
You shade black squares on a fresh sheet of graph paper, aiming for something that looks like a real Kakuro grid. Halfway through filling in digits you notice three problems. A white cell in the corner has a down clue but nothing across. One row runs ten cells long. And a little 2x2 pocket in the lower left doesn’t touch anything else.

None of those can be fixed with better digits. The layout was broken before you wrote a single number.

The pattern of black and white squares decides most of how a Kakuro plays: where the solver can start, how long each run is, and where a second solution can hide. This article covers the layout rules every published Kakuro follows, how symmetry works, what black cells and run lengths do to the solve, and then builds the 7x7 layout used throughout this series, one pair of black cells at a time.

The Layout Rules

Runs Are 2 to 9 Cells

A run is an unbroken line of white cells under one clue. Two limits apply.

A one-cell run is out. Its clue would just be the answer, printed in plain sight. Published Kakuro doesn’t use them, and a grid full of them would be a fill-in exercise.

A run can’t be longer than nine cells either. Digits can’t repeat within a run, and there are only nine digits. A ten-cell run has no legal fill. A nine-cell run is always 1 through 9 and always sums to 45, which makes it the one place in Kakuro where the number 45 is guaranteed.

The short end of the range does a lot of work. Two-cell runs make good starting points because several of their sums allow only one pair of digits: 3 is {1, 2}, 4 is {1, 3}, 16 is {7, 9} and 17 is {8, 9}.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  4\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+

That white cell is boxed in on all sides. Its across run and its down run are each one cell long, so both clues just say 4. There’s nothing to deduce.

Every White Cell Is Crossed Both Ways, and Everything Connects

Every white cell belongs to exactly one across run and exactly one down run. A cell with black squares directly above and below it has no down run, so nothing checks its digit from that direction. That’s the corner cell from the opening.

All the white cells must also form one connected piece. Cells that touch only at a corner don’t count. A cut-off pocket is a separate puzzle with no way for logic to get in or out, and it usually has several solutions.

180° Rotational Symmetry

How It Works

Turn a symmetric grid upside down and the black-and-white pattern looks the same. Every black cell has a partner on the opposite side of the center.

Symmetry isn’t one of Kakuro’s rules. Nikoli’s rule list has three entries, and none mentions layout. It’s a convention, and a strong one in hand-made grids, because a balanced layout looks deliberate and tends to spread the solving evenly across the page.

Measure symmetry on the interior, not the clue border. The top row and left column are all clue cells. Turn the full grid and they’d land on the bottom and right edges, so no grid would ever pass. Leave the border out.

In the series grid, the full grid is 7x7, the interior is rows 1–6 and columns 1–6, and interior cell (r, c) pairs with (7 − r, 7 − c). In general, for an N×N grid with the border at row 0 and column 0, the partner of (r, c) is (N − r, N − c). Two examples from the series layout: the black cell at r3c3 pairs with r4c4, and r1c5 pairs with r6c2.

The Trade-Offs

Symmetry costs flexibility. Every black cell you add brings a partner, so a fix in the top-left changes the bottom-right too, and the partner might break a run that was fine.

Odd-sized interiors have one more wrinkle. In a 7x7 interior (an 8x8 grid with its border), the center cell pairs with itself. Decide early whether it’s black or white: a white center makes a crossroads in the middle of the grid, while a black one splits the grid into four regions that meet around it.

Some puzzles break symmetry on purpose. An escape-room grid shaped like a keyhole, or a themed puzzle that spells something in black cells, trades the convention for a reason. Do it deliberately, not by accident.

Black Cells

How Many

With too few black cells, runs get long, sums get large, and every clue has dozens of combinations. Long runs also leave room for second solutions. With too many, the grid breaks into short, easy runs, and the puzzle turns choppy.

When you quote a percentage, say what you’re counting. The series grid is 51% black overall: 25 of its 49 cells. But 13 of those are the border, which every grid has. Count only the interior and it’s 12 of 36, or 33%. Both numbers describe the same grid, and only the second tells you much about how it will play.

Where They Go

The top row and left column hold clues. Past that, three placement habits matter:

  • Avoid one-cell bridges. If two big sections connect through a single white cell, all the logic has to squeeze through it.
  • Keep the middle open enough to carry logic across. A solid wall of black cells through the center makes two separate puzzles that happen to share a page.
  • Watch the 2x2 white blocks. Any 2x2 block of white cells is a place where four digits can swap and give a second solution. The series layout has eight of them. They aren’t errors, but each is a spot to check later. How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution covers what to look for.

Run Lengths and How the Solve Moves

Short Runs (2–3 Cells)

Short runs are where solvers start. Four two-cell sums have a single combination (3, 4, 16, 17), and so do four three-cell sums (6 is {1, 2, 3}, 7 is {1, 2, 4}, 23 is {6, 8, 9}, 24 is {7, 8, 9}). Even when a short run’s sum has several options, the options are few enough to compare quickly.

Run length Possible sums Sums with only one digit set
2 cells 3–17 3, 4, 16, 17
3 cells 6–24 6, 7, 23, 24
4 cells 10–30 10, 11, 29, 30
5 cells 15–35 15, 16, 34, 35

Put a few short runs near the edges and corners, and the solver has somewhere to begin.

Longer Runs (4+ Cells)

Four- and five-cell runs carry the middle of the solve. They connect the short runs and pass information across the grid. They rarely give up a digit on their own, so they rely on the runs crossing them. In the series grid, the row-5 across run is four cells long and is crossed by four down runs, one of them only two cells long. That short crossing is what pins it down.

On a small grid, keep runs short. The series layout tops out at four cells, which suits a 7x7.

Practical Example: Drafting the Series 7x7 Layout

You’re building the blank layout used for the rest of this series. The goals:

  • 7x7 including the clue border, leaving a 6x6 interior
  • 180° symmetry on the interior: (r, c) pairs with (7 − r, 7 − c)
  • No one-cell runs, every white cell crossed both ways, everything connected
  • A mix of 2-, 3- and 4-cell runs

Step 1: Black out the border. Row 0 and column 0 become clue cells.

Step 2: Black out the top-right and bottom-left corners. Shade r1c5, r1c6, r2c5 and r2c6, then their partners r6c2, r6c1, r5c2 and r5c1. That cuts off the interior’s top-right and bottom-left corners and leaves a wide band of white cells running diagonally from top-left to bottom-right.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Rows 3 and 4 still run six cells wide, which is too long for a grid this size.

Step 3: Split the middle. Shade r3c3 and its partner r4c4. Rows 3 and 4 now break into shorter runs, and columns 3 and 4 split top from bottom.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |#######|       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |#######|       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 4: Trim the edges. Shade r3c6 and its partner r4c1. That shortens the row-3 and row-4 runs at the edges and keeps the column-1 and column-6 runs to three cells.

Step 5: Check everything. Trace every row and every column for a one-cell run. Confirm every white cell has both an across and a down run. Walk the white cells to confirm they connect. Then turn the page upside down and compare the interior.

Every pair you place goes through the same loop:

The finished layout:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|       |       |#######|       |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|       |       |#######|       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

You should get 24 white cells and 25 black ones (13 border, 12 interior), and 16 runs: six of 2 cells, four of 3 and six of 4. There’s a printable version, kakuro-series-layout-7x7.pdf, with the clue cells marked and the center of rotation shown.

Printable Templates

Graph paper works, but it doesn’t mark the border or show you where the center is. These US Letter PDFs do:

  • Series layout, 7x7: the layout above, clue cells marked
  • Design grid, 7x7: small, for quick puzzles and practice
  • Design grid, 10x10 and 12x12: typical puzzle-book sizes
  • Design grid, 15x15: for large, expert-level grids
  • Series puzzles, Medium and Hard: the finished series grids, ready to solve
  • All templates in one file (7 pages)

Each design grid has the clue border pre-marked, row and column numbers that match the (r, c) notation used here, a dot at the center of rotation, and the pairing rule (r, c) ↔ (N − r, N − c) printed at the bottom.

Best Practices

Do:

  • ✓ Place black cells in pairs, and check the partner every time.
  • ✓ Put at least two short runs near the corners so the solver has a way in.
  • ✓ Trace every row and column for one-cell runs after each change.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Trap a white cell between black squares in one direction.
  • ✗ Wall off a section of the grid.
  • ✗ Quote a black-cell percentage without saying whether the border counts.

Troubleshooting Layout Problems

A white cell has no down run. There’s a black cell directly above it and another directly below. Move one of them, or turn the cell black (along with its partner). After any change, check each column top to bottom.

The layout stops being symmetric after an edit. You changed one cell and forgot its partner. Always edit in pairs, (r, c) and (N − r, N − c). Keeping a list of pairs next to the grid while you work makes this hard to forget.

Moving a black cell created a one-cell run somewhere else. Shifting a black cell to shorten one run can leave a one-cell stub in the crossing direction. Check both the row and the column after every move, not just the run you were fixing.

What Comes Next

Layout comes first, because most layout problems can’t be fixed later with digits. Keep runs between two and nine cells, cross every white cell both ways, connect everything, and measure symmetry on the interior. Black cells decide where the solver starts and where swaps can hide.

Print the series layout, or grab a blank design grid and sketch your own. The next step is filling the layout with digits and making sure only one solution comes out: How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution.

You’re twenty minutes into a hard Kakuro, and you’ve just worked out 17 in two cells for the third time tonight. 9 and 8. You knew that. You also knew it the last two times, and you still ran the arithmetic, because the habit hasn’t moved from your head to your eyes yet.

That small tax adds up. Every sum you recompute is attention you don’t spend on the part of the grid that’s hard. Solvers who move fast on expert grids aren’t doing faster mental math. They’ve stopped doing math for a short list of clues, because those clues have exactly one answer and they recognize them on sight.

Conceptis Puzzles calls these clues magic blocks: a clue and a cell count that only one set of digits can satisfy. Entries of two to five cells have just sixteen magic blocks in total, and you already know a few.

2-Cell Magic Blocks

The Extremes

Two rules create every magic block. You only get digits 1 through 9, and no digit can repeat inside a single entry (the run of white cells one clue covers). Those two rules pinch the ends of the number range.

The smallest sum two different digits can make is 1 + 2 = 3. The largest is 9 + 8 = 17. One step in from each end, you still have one option, because the alternative needs a repeat:

Clue Cells Only combination Why
3 2 {1, 2} Nothing smaller exists
4 2 {1, 3} 2 + 2 repeats
16 2 {7, 9} 8 + 8 repeats
17 2 {8, 9} Nothing larger exists

These four are your primary entry points because two-cell entries are the most common entries in almost every grid. If you have only memorized one set, make it this one. A shortcut: the high pairs mirror the low pairs around 10. Swap 1 for 9, 2 for 8, 3 for 7, and {1, 2} becomes {9, 8} while {1, 3} becomes {9, 7}.

Near-Extremes

One more step toward the middle, the options split in two. 5 in two cells is {1, 4} or {2, 3}. 15 in two cells is {6, 9} or {7, 8}. Neither is a magic block, and treating them like one is the most common cheat-sheet error.

Near-extremes still do work for you. A 5 can never hold a digit above 4, and one known digit settles the other. A 5 is also always one odd digit plus one even digit, since an odd total from two cells needs one of each. If a crossing clue tells you one cell is odd, the other is even, and that alone often decides which pair you’re looking at.

3-Cell Magic Blocks

Low End Combinations

Three cells give you four more:

Clue Cells Only combination
6 3 {1, 2, 3}
7 3 {1, 2, 4}
23 3 {6, 8, 9}
24 3 {7, 8, 9}

The low pair, 6 and 7, does its best work in corners. A corner cell sits at the start of both an across entry and a down entry, so it collects two constraints at once. Put a 7-in-three across a 4-in-two down and the shared cell has to come from {1, 2, 4} and {1, 3} at the same time. Only 1 survives.

High End Combinations

23 and 24 work the other way. Every cell in a 24 is 7 or higher, so each crossing entry loses its low digits at that cell. If a 24-in-three crosses a 12-in-two, the 12 could be {3, 9}, {4, 8}, or {5, 7}, but the shared cell can’t be 3, 4, or 5. It has to take the big half of whichever pair it is, and the 12’s other cell has to take the small half. Six candidates in the shared cell become three, and you haven’t written a single pencil mark.

Larger Block Extremes (4 & 5 Cells)

The 4-Cell Constants

Four cells have magic blocks at 10 {1, 2, 3, 4}, 11 {1, 2, 3, 5}, 29 {5, 7, 8, 9}, and 30 {6, 7, 8, 9}.

A 10 in four cells is a wall of small digits. Every cell in it is 4 or lower, so every entry that crosses it gets a cell capped at 4. A crossing 16-in-two {7, 9} can’t share a cell with it at all, and a valid puzzle will never ask it to. A crossing 9-in-two {1, 8}, {2, 7}, {3, 6}, {4, 5} keeps all four pairs, but its shared cell is forced to the small half of each.

The 5-Cell Constants

Five cells have four magic blocks too: 15 {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, 16 {1, 2, 3, 4, 6}, 34 {4, 6, 7, 8, 9}, and 35 {5, 6, 7, 8, 9}. Most cheat sheets skip 16 and 34. Don’t: the worked example on Conceptis’ techniques page uses a 16 in five cells.

Five-cell blocks rarely hand you a digit by themselves. Their value is subtraction. Once the ends of a 15 are filled, the middle three come from whatever’s left of 1 through 5, and that leftover set is usually small enough to finish with one crossing clue.

Practical Example: Finding Entry Points

Here is a blank grid. Clue cells read down\across: 4\ is a down clue of 4, \15 is an across clue of 15, and 16\4 holds a down 16 and an across 4.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  4\   | 20\   |#######| 20\   |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |       |       | 16\4  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \15 |       |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\6  |       |       |       | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \35 |       |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |       |       |   \16 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 1: Scan every across clue. Count each entry’s cells and check the clue against your list. You find \3 (2 cells), \4 (2 cells), \15 (5 cells), \6 (3 cells), \35 (5 cells), \17 (2 cells), and \16 (2 cells). All seven across clues are magic blocks.

Step 2: Scan every down clue. 4\ (2 cells), 3\ (2 cells), 16\ (2 cells, bottom left), and 17\ (2 cells, bottom right) are magic. The two 20s in five cells and the 16 in three cells are not.

Step 3: Pencil in the sets. Where a cell sits in two magic blocks, write only the digits both blocks allow:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  4\   | 20\   |#######| 20\   |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |  1 2  | 16\4  |  1 3  |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \15 |  1 3  |  1-5  |  1-5  |  1-5  |  1 2  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\6  | 1 2 3 | 1 2 3 | 1 2 3 | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \35 |  7 9  |  5-9  |  5-9  |  5-9  |  8 9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |  8 9  |   \16 |  7 9  |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

All four corners collapse at once. Top left: the across 3 allows {1, 2}, the down 4 allows {1, 3}, and the only shared digit is 1. Top right is the mirror: 4 across {1, 3} against 3 down {1, 2}, so 1 again. The bottom corners do the same thing at the high end, with 17 against 16 leaving 9 both times.

Each corner digit finishes its partners. The 3 across needs a 2 next to the 1. The 4 down needs a 3 under it. Work all four corners and the grid fills in fast:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  4\   | 20\   |#######| 20\   |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 16\4  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \15 |   3   | 1 4 5 | 1 4 5 | 1 4 5 |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\6  |  1 3  | 1 2 3 |  1 2  | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \35 |   7   | 5 6 9 | 5 6 9 | 5 6 9 |   8   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   8   |   \16 |   7   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The five-cell rows paid off exactly as promised. Row two already holds 3 and 2, so its middle is {1, 4, 5}. Row four holds 7 and 8, so its middle is {5, 6, 9}. In row three, the column above has already used a 2 in column two and a 3 in column four, so those two cells drop to {1, 3} and {1, 2}.

Twelve cells are solved and you haven’t added a single non-magic clue. The finish takes one sum. The right-hand 20 down already holds 3 and 7, so its middle three cells total 10, with one cell from {1, 4, 5}, one from {1, 2}, and one from {5, 6, 9}. Only 4 + 1 + 5 works. That 1 finishes row three as 3, 2, 1, and the left-hand 20 down then needs its two open cells to total 7, which only 1 + 6 manages.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  4\   | 20\   |#######| 20\   |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 16\4  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \15 |   3   |   1   |   5   |   4   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\6  |   3   |   2   |   1   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \35 |   7   |   6   |   9   |   5   |   8   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   8   |   \16 |   7   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Best Practices and Tips

Do:

  • ✓ Memorize the 2-cell and 3-cell extremes first: 3, 4, 16, 17 and 6, 7, 23, 24. They appear in nearly every grid.
  • ✓ Keep a printed cheat sheet next to the puzzle until you stop glancing at it.
  • ✓ Look for cells where two magic blocks cross before anything else. That’s where digits appear for free.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Try to memorize every combination for mid-range sums. 13 in three cells has seven different sets. Work those out when you need them.
  • ✗ Commit a digit to a magic block cell before checking the crossing clue.

Speed tip: Make flashcards with the clue and cell count on the front (for example, “23 / 3”) and the set on the back. A few minutes a day covers the 2- and 3-cell blocks faster than you’d expect.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

“I know the combination, but not the order.”

  • Cause: Neither cell has a crossing constraint yet.
  • Fix: Leave both digits as small pencil marks in both cells and work elsewhere. The crossing entry will eventually take one option away.
  • Prevention: Don’t guess the order. Half the time you’ll be wrong, and you won’t find out until ten moves later.

“My magic block came out with the wrong digits.”

  • Cause: You miscounted the cells. 16 in two cells is {7, 9}. 16 in three cells has eight possible sets.
  • Fix: Count the white cells between the clue and the next black square before reaching for the cheat sheet.

“I treated 5 or 15 as unique.”

  • Cause: Near-extremes look like magic blocks.
  • Fix: 5 in two cells is {1, 4} or {2, 3}, and 15 is {6, 9} or {7, 8}. Pencil both pairs and let a crossing clue choose.

The Full Cheat Sheet

Cells Low magic blocks High magic blocks
2 3 {1,2} · 4 {1,3} 16 {7,9} · 17 {8,9}
3 6 {1,2,3} · 7 {1,2,4} 23 {6,8,9} · 24 {7,8,9}
4 10 {1,2,3,4} · 11 {1,2,3,5} 29 {5,7,8,9} · 30 {6,7,8,9}
5 15 {1,2,3,4,5} · 16 {1,2,3,4,6} 34 {4,6,7,8,9} · 35 {5,6,7,8,9}

Longer entries have magic blocks too, and the 45 Rule shows you how to read them without another table.

Conclusion

Key takeaways:

  1. Magic blocks are your entry points. Every expert solve starts with them.
  2. For two cells, 3, 4, 16, and 17 are the ones that matter most.
  3. For three cells, learn 6, 7, 23, and 24.
  4. The win is recognition, not arithmetic. Once you see the clue and the set together, you stop paying the math tax.

Next steps: Print the cheat sheet and keep it beside your next puzzle. When the corners start falling without it, move on to reading what happens where entries cross.

content:
You open the puzzle book to the Kakuro page, uncap the pen, and look at the first clue cell. It holds two numbers, 24 and 16, separated by a diagonal line. Which one goes with the row? You pick the 24, spend five minutes building a combination that adds up to it across two cells, and realize two cells can’t add up to more than 17. The math was fine. You just solved the wrong clue.

Half the difficulty of a first Kakuro isn’t arithmetic. It’s figuring out what the grid is asking. The rules are short, but each one carries a detail that’s easy to misread, and one misread rule will quietly wreck an entire solve.

The Core Rules of Kakuro

Nikoli, the Japanese publisher that gave Kakuro its name, states the rules in three lines:

  1. Put numbers from 1 through 9 in each cell (no zeros).
  2. A number in a cell divided by a diagonal line tells the sum of the numbers in the consecutive cells to its right or downward.
  3. No number may appear more than once in consecutive cells.

That’s the whole rulebook. Everything else is a consequence of those three lines, and each line hides a detail worth spelling out.

The Objective and the Numbers

The goal is to fill every white cell on the board. Each one takes a single digit from 1 to 9. A 0 isn’t allowed, and neither is a 10 or anything larger.

If you’ve played Sudoku, the digit range looks familiar, but the digits behave differently. In Sudoku, the numbers are labels. You could swap them for nine colors and the puzzle would work the same way. In Kakuro, the digits are quantities. A 9 is worth more than a 1, and every clue depends on that. The 1-to-9 limit is also what makes Kakuro solvable at all. With only nine digits and no repeats inside an entry, most clues have a short list of possible answers, and some have just one.

The “No Duplicates” Rule

This rule decides more solves than any other: a digit cannot repeat within a single entry.

Take a clue of 4 across two cells. Arithmetic offers two answers, 1 + 3 and 2 + 2. Only one of them is legal.

Valid:    [\4 ][ 1 ][ 3 ]     1 + 3 = 4, no repeats
Invalid:  [\4 ][ 2 ][ 2 ]     2 + 2 = 4, but the 2 repeats

The same rule applies to longer entries. A clue of 7 across three cells can be [1][2][4]. It can’t be [2][3][2], even though that also adds to 7. Once you rule out repeats, 1 + 2 + 4 turns out to be the only way to make 7 in three cells, and that kind of shortcut is where solving starts.

The scope matters. The rule covers one entry, not the whole row. If a black cell splits a row into two separate entries, the same digit can appear in both:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \7  |   4   |   3   |   \13 |   4   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Two 4s in one row, and both are legal. The first 4 belongs to the across 7 (4 + 3). The second belongs to the across 13 (4 + 9). The black cell between them ends one entry and starts the next.

Reading the Grid Anatomy

Clues and Black Squares

Black cells do two jobs: they hold clues, and they mark where entries end. A black cell with clues is split by a diagonal line running from top-left to bottom-right, which leaves two triangles.

  • The number in the top-right triangle is an across clue. It applies to the white cells running to the right.
  • The number in the bottom-left triangle is a down clue. It applies to the white cells running down.

Clues only ever point right or down, never left or up. A memory aid: each number sits on the side of the diagonal closest to the cells it describes. The top-right number sits beside the row, and the bottom-left number sits above the column.

In this series, clue cells are written as down\across, matching the diagonal: the down clue sits before the slash, the across clue after it.

+-------+-------+-------+
| 24\16 |   →   |   →   |    16 = sum of the two cells to the right
+-------+-------+-------+
|   ↓   |
+-------+
|   ↓   |
+-------+
|   ↓   |
+-------+
  24 = sum of the three cells below

The 24\16 cell holds two clues. The 16 is the across clue, so the two cells to its right have to add up to 16. The 24 is the down clue, so the three cells below it have to add up to 24. A cell with a single number works the same way: what matters is which side of the diagonal it’s on, not how many numbers the cell holds.

To trace an entry, put your finger on the clue cell and slide right (for an across clue) or down (for a down clue). Count every white cell until you hit a black cell or the edge of the grid. That count is the entry length, and you need it before you can do any math.

Entries and Bounds

An entry (some sources call it a “run” or “block”) is one unbroken line of white cells. It begins right after its clue cell and ends at the next black cell or the grid edge.

Entries are at least two cells long. A one-cell entry would hand you its answer outright, since the cell would simply equal its clue, so puzzles don’t use them. Entries can be up to nine cells long, and a nine-cell entry must contain every digit from 1 to 9 exactly once, which always adds to 45.

Length decides the math. Compare a 3-cell entry and a 5-cell entry, both with a clue of 15:

3-cell:  [\15][   ][   ][   ]                 eight possible digit sets
5-cell:  [\15][   ][   ][   ][   ][   ]       one possible set: 1+2+3+4+5

The 3-cell version could be {1,5,9}, {2,6,7}, {4,5,6}, or five other sets. The 5-cell version has no freedom at all: five different digits can’t add up to less than 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15, so that’s the only answer. Same clue, opposite difficulty, and the only difference is how many cells you counted.

This is why counting comes first. If you misjudge an entry’s length by one cell, every combination you build is wrong from the start.

Do’s and Don’ts

Do:

  • ✓ Trace the length of an entry with your finger before doing any arithmetic.
  • ✓ Check that you haven’t repeated a digit before you finalize an entry.
  • ✓ Read every clue cell by its position: top-right goes across, bottom-left goes down.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Mix up across and down clues, especially in cells that hold only one number.
  • ✗ Assume an entry spans the whole row. A black cell in the middle ends it.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

“I placed a 5 and a 5 in the same row. Is that a mistake?” Not if a black cell separates them. The no-duplicates rule applies to each entry on its own, not to the full row or column. Two 5s in the same row are fine as long as they sit in different entries. To keep it straight, think in entries, not rows. Before you check for repeats, find the black cells at both ends of the entry and only look between them.

“My combination adds up, but it can’t fit the cells.” You’ve probably read a down clue as an across clue, or the other way around. This happens most with clue cells that hold a single number. Check which triangle the number sits in. If it’s bottom-left, the clue runs down, even if the cells to the right are empty and inviting.

“The clue is bigger than any possible sum.” Two cells top out at 17 (9 + 8), three cells at 24, four at 30. If a clue seems too big for its entry, you’ve counted the length wrong or you’re reading the wrong clue. Re-trace from the clue cell.

Conclusion

Kakuro’s rules fit on an index card, but every one has a catch. Get these right and the logic techniques in the rest of this series will actually work.

Key takeaways:

  1. Only digits 1 through 9 are allowed. No zeros, no two-digit numbers.
  2. No digit repeats within a single entry, but the same digit can appear twice in a row if a black cell separates the two entries.
  3. Top-right clues run across to the right. Bottom-left clues run down.
  4. Entries are bounded by black cells or the grid edge, and their length controls which combinations are possible.

Next steps: With the rules settled, you’re ready for your first real solving technique: finding the clues that have only one possible answer.

You spot a two-letter word that starts with the free T. It has to be TO. You fill in the O, and suddenly an eight-letter word reads T _ _ O _ _ _ _ and your brain refuses to let it go. Five minutes later you’re muttering at a 135-year-old sentence about evidence. That’s the cryptogram effect: one right guess pays for itself everywhere the letter appears.

Every letter in the quote below has been swapped for a different letter, and the swap holds for the whole puzzle. If K means E once, it means E every time. No letter ever stands for itself. You get one letter free.

The cipher

Loading puzzle...

How to play

  • Tap any box and type a letter. Every box sharing that cipher letter fills in at the same time.
  • Arrow keys move between boxes; Backspace clears a letter (all copies of it).
  • The alphabet strip under the quote greys out letters you’ve already used, so you can see what’s left at a glance.
  • A guess that’s already on another cipher letter turns orange, a gentle nudge that two letters can’t share an answer.
  • Check Solution marks wrong letters in red and counts as a mistake. Reveal a Letter fills in the most common letter you haven’t cracked yet.

Stuck?

  1. Hunt the short words. One-letter words are almost always A or I. Two- and three-letter words like TO, OF, IS, THE and ONE give you a foothold fast.
  2. Follow the repeats. Three words in the second sentence each appear twice. Matching letter patterns in long words are a gift.
  3. Count. E, T, A, O, I and N are the most common letters in English, a fact Edgar Allan Poe’s hero uses in “The Gold-Bug” (1843) to crack a pirate’s cipher. Find the cipher letters that turn up most often in the quote and try those first.

The quote keeps its original 1891 British spelling, so don’t fight it when a word lands one letter off from what you expect.
