Your first Kakuro is finished. The sums are clean, the layout is symmetric, and every run adds up. Your test solver works through the grid and stops near the bottom. Four cells: 9 and 8 on top, 8 and 9 underneath. Or 8 and 9 on top, 9 and 8 underneath. Every clue checks out both ways. One of the runs through those cells is a 17 in two cells, which you’d have sworn locked them down.

It didn’t. Your puzzle has two answers.

A Kakuro is supposed to have exactly one answer, reachable by logic alone. A second solution means that somewhere the solver has to guess, and the cause is almost always the same: a group of cells whose digits can trade places without any clue noticing. This article takes the series 7x7 layout from Designing a Kakuro Grid, fills it, finds that trade, shows why the obvious fix fails, and repairs it with a single digit.

Why Grids End Up with Two Solutions

The Deal with the Solver

When someone sits down with your puzzle, they’re trusting that every cell has exactly one correct digit and that logic will lead them to it. Nikoli’s rule list doesn’t spell this out, but published Kakuro is built on it. A puzzle with two answers breaks it. The solver reaches the ambiguous cells, finds nothing that decides them, and either guesses or gives up. Either way, the last few minutes of the solve, usually the most satisfying part, turn into a coin toss.

Fill-First Hides the Problem

If you build fill-first, writing digits into the layout and then adding up the clues, you know one solution exists because you wrote it. That tells you nothing about whether a second one exists. Wikipedia’s Kakuro article puts the source of uniqueness plainly: it’s the ban on repeated digits within a run that makes unique solutions possible at all. Nothing else in the rules pins digits in place.

Clue-first construction catches more of these as you go, because you’re solving while you build. But even clue-first constructors check the finished grid, and the check starts with knowing what to look for.

Anatomy of a Swap

The 2x2 Swap

Here’s the first fill of the series grid. The four cells in brackets are the ones from the opening.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |   6   |   3   |   2   |   1   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   9   |   6   |   8   |   4   | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 24\8  |   3   |   5   |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |   1   |   7   | 17\8  |   6   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \21 |  [9]  |  [8]  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |  [8]  |  [9]  |   7   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

And here’s the second solution, with only those four cells changed:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |   6   |   3   |   2   |   1   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   9   |   6   |   8   |   4   | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 24\8  |   3   |   5   |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |   1   |   7   | 17\8  |   6   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \21 |  [8]  |  [9]  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |  [9]  |  [8]  |   7   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The four cells r5c3, r5c4, r6c3 and r6c4 sit at the corners of a rectangle: two across runs and two down runs pass through them. They hold A B on top and B A below. Flip them to B A over A B and look at each run:

Run Version 1 Version 2
21 across (row 5) {9, 8, 3, 1} {8, 9, 3, 1}
27 across (row 6) {8, 9, 7, 3} {9, 8, 7, 3}
24 down (column 3) {7, 9, 8} {7, 8, 9}
17 down (column 4) {8, 9} {9, 8}

Every run holds exactly the same digits both ways. Only the order changes. Sums don’t care about order and neither does the no-repeat rule, so no clue can tell the two versions apart. Puzzle constructors call this a deadly pattern. In this series it’s a swap.

Why a Magic Block Doesn’t Help

Look again at the table. Two of the four runs are magic blocks, clues with only one possible digit set: 24 in three cells is always {7, 8, 9}, and 17 in two cells is always {8, 9}. The swap survives both of them.

A magic block fixes which digits a run uses. It says nothing about where they go. A swap changes only where they go. So the most tempting fix, “make one of those runs a magic block so it’s locked down,” does nothing against a pure swap. The draft already had two magic blocks there, and the swap went straight through.

Shifted Swaps and Longer Loops

A pure swap trades two digits. A looser version adds an amount to two opposite corners and takes it from the other two. Picture a rectangle holding 1 4 over 2 3. Add 1 to the top-left and bottom-right, subtract 1 from the other two, and you get 2 3 over 1 4. Every sum is unchanged, but some runs now hold different digits: the top row went from {1, 4} to {2, 3}. A shifted swap can be caught by a clue, because a magic block or a digit already used elsewhere in the run can rule out the new set.

Swaps don’t have to be rectangles, either. Six cells across three rows and three columns can do it:

 +d   -d    .
  .   +d   -d
 -d    .   +d

Each row gains d once and loses it once, and so does each column, so every sum holds. Loops of eight cells or more work the same way. They’re rarer and harder to spot, which is a good reason to let a computer double-check you (see Build a Kakuro Solver and Generator in Python).

How to Fix It

Fix 1: Change a Digit, Then Recalculate Its Clues

In Kakuro, a clue is the sum of the digits beneath it. You can’t change a clue without changing the solution under it, so the real edit is always to a digit. Change one digit, then recalculate both clues that run through it.

For the series grid, change r5c3 from 9 to 4:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |   6   |   3   |   2   |   1   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   9   |   6   |   8   |   4   | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 19\8  |   3   |   5   |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |   1   |   7   | 17\8  |   6   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |  [4]  |   8   |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |   8   |   9   |   7   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Two clues change. Row 5’s across goes from 21 to 16 (4 + 8 + 3 + 1), and column 3’s lower down run goes from 24 to 19 (7 + 4 + 8).

Why it works: the corners no longer hold A B over B A, so a plain swap is gone. The only shift left would need r5c3 = 3, r5c4 = 9, r6c3 = 9 and r6c4 = 8 to keep every sum the same. That puts a second 3 in row 5, where r5c5 is already 3. The no-repeat rule kills it.

Also notice what didn’t change: the 17 down is still a magic block. It wasn’t the fix. The new digit was.

Fix 2: Move a Black Cell

Splitting one of the four runs breaks the rectangle, because the corners no longer share both an across run and a down run. It’s a bigger edit. The black cell has a symmetry partner, so you’re moving two cells and changing the shape of four or more runs. Reach for it when digit changes keep opening new problems elsewhere, or when a big open area keeps producing swaps no matter what you write in it.

Proving Uniqueness by Hand

Solve It with Forced Moves Only

The cleanest proof needs nothing but a pencil. Solve your puzzle from blank, and only write a digit when it’s the only possibility at that moment. If you can fill every cell that way, the solution is unique. Every step had exactly one option, so there was never room for a second answer.

Here’s how the repaired series grid starts:

  1. r6c6 = 3. The 6 down along the right edge is three cells, so it’s {1, 2, 3}. The 27 across on row 6 is four cells: {3, 7, 8, 9}, {4, 6, 8, 9} or {5, 6, 7, 9}. The corner cell belongs to both, and 3 is the only digit they share.
  2. Row 6 is {3, 7, 8, 9}. It’s the only 27-in-four set with a 3, so r6c3, r6c4 and r6c5 hold 7, 8 and 9 in some order.
  3. r2c2 = 6. The 27 across on row 2 needs four digits from 3 up. But r2c2 also sits in the 12-down in column 2, which is {1, 2, 3, 6} or {1, 2, 4, 5}, so r2c2 is at most 6. And r2c4 sits in the 8-down in column 4, {1, 2, 5} or {1, 3, 4}, so it’s at most 5. Try each 27 set: {3, 7, 8, 9} would need both of those cells to be 3, which can’t happen. The other two sets, {4, 6, 8, 9} and {5, 6, 7, 9}, both force r2c2 = 6.

Every other cell falls the same way, one forced move at a time, with no guessing. That’s the proof.

When You Get Stuck: Test Both Options

Sometimes you stall and can’t tell whether you’ve missed a deduction or the puzzle is ambiguous. Pick a cell with two candidates and follow each one forward. If one leads to a contradiction, like a repeated digit or a sum that can’t be reached, the other is forced and you can keep going. If both lead to a complete, valid grid, you’ve found a second solution.

Run that test on the draft and it stalls at the four bracketed cells, each one either 8 or 9. Try r5c3 = 9: the grid completes. Try r5c3 = 8: it completes again. Two solutions, confirmed.

The common mistake is stopping after the first branch works. A branch that finishes proves one solution exists. Only a branch that fails tells you anything about uniqueness.

Put together, the whole hand check looks like this:

Practical Example: From Draft to Main

Here’s the whole repair as a checklist you can run on your own grid.

  1. Find the second solution. Test-solve the draft. At the stall, test both options on one of the four bottom cells. Both finish, so the draft has two solutions.
  2. Identify the four cells. r5c3, r5c4, r6c3, r6c4, holding 9 8 over 8 9.
  3. Check the runs. Each of the four runs holds the same digits in both versions. Two of them (24 down, 17 down) are magic blocks, and they don’t stop it.
  4. Change one corner digit. r5c3 from 9 to 4. Recalculate the two clues through it: row 5 becomes 16, column 3’s lower run becomes 19.
  5. Prove it. Solve the new grid with forced moves only, starting with r6c6 = 3. Every cell falls without a guess.

The result is the series Main puzzle:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |       |       |       |       | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |       |       | 19\8  |       |       |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |       |       | 17\8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

One solution, every move forced. It’s in the printable series puzzles if you’d rather solve it on paper.

Best Practices

Do:

  • ✓ Check every 2x2 block of white cells for matching digits on opposite corners.
  • ✓ Test-solve with forced moves only, and treat any guess as a red flag.
  • ✓ When you change a digit, recalculate both clues through it.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Assume a puzzle is unique because you solved it. You knew the answer.
  • ✗ Expect a magic block to stop a pure swap.
  • ✗ Change a clue without changing the digits underneath.

Troubleshooting

The swap is still there after a change. The change kept the A B over B A pattern. Maybe you swapped which corners held which digit, or changed digits outside the rectangle. Change one of the four corner digits to something new, so the corners no longer mirror each other.

The fix created a problem somewhere else. The new digit repeats in a crossing run, or the new clue opens a different swap elsewhere. Re-check both runs through the changed cell, then re-solve the whole grid from blank, not just the corner you fixed.

You fixed one swap and the grid still has two solutions. There was a second, independent swap in another part of the grid. Two separate swaps give four solutions, and fixing one leaves two. Keep testing until a forced-only solve runs start to finish.

Where This Leaves You

A valid fill proves a solution exists, not that it’s the only one. In a pure swap every run keeps the same digits, so no clue can catch it, and that includes magic blocks. Fix a swap by changing a digit and recalculating its two clues, or by moving a black cell. Then prove the result by solving it with forced moves only.

title: How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution

content:
You’ve hit a wall in an expert Kakuro. Every magic block on the page is filled in, every easy crossing is done, and a fat block of empty cells is sitting in the middle of the grid. Each clue around it has five or six workable combinations. You pencil a few, erase them, and pencil them again.

If you’ve played Killer Sudoku, your hand goes to the 45 rule. Every 3×3 box holds 1 through 9, so add up the cages, subtract from 45, and the missing cell falls out. You try it here, and you get 13 for a single cell.

Nothing is wrong with your arithmetic. You’ve hit the one place where the Sudoku version of the rule doesn’t carry over. A Kakuro block has no duty to hold 1 through 9. The idea underneath the 45 rule does carry over, though, and in Kakuro it’s even simpler.

The Foundation of the 45 Rule

The Math Explained

1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 = 45. Any region that has to contain each digit exactly once must sum to 45, which is why the rule works in Killer Sudoku, where every row, column, and box is such a region.

Kakuro only promises no repeats within a single entry, the run of white cells under one clue. Two different entries can reuse the same digits as often as they like. Fill an open 3×3 block like this and every row and column is legal:

1 2 3
2 3 1
3 1 2

That block sums to 18, not 45. So in Kakuro, 45 is guaranteed in exactly one place: an entry nine cells long. That clue is always 45 (Wikipedia notes the clue is simply written “45”, because the nine cells are implied), and it tells you nothing about order.

Finding the Remainder

The literal 45 becomes useful one step down. An eight-cell entry uses eight of the nine digits, so the one it skips is 45 minus the clue. A 38 in eight cells is missing 7. A 44 is missing 1. Every eight-cell clue from 36 to 44 is a magic block. You just read it through a subtraction instead of a table.

The same trick works for shorter long entries:

Entry Clue 45 − clue Missing digits Digits used
8 cells 38 7 {7} {1,2,3,4,5,6,8,9}
7 cells 41 4 {1,3} {2,4,5,6,7,8,9}
7 cells 30 15 {6,9} or {7,8} two options
6 cells 39 6 {1,2,3} {4,5,6,7,8,9}

Read the table sideways and you’ll see that a long entry is a short entry in disguise. A 41 in seven cells is just “4 in two cells”, turned inside out, and you already know that’s {1, 3}. The 30-in-seven row matches the example Wikipedia uses to show that 30 in seven cells has exactly two possible sets.

Innies and Outies

The bigger idea behind the 45 rule isn’t 45. It’s counting the same cells twice.

Pick a region of the grid. Add every across clue whose entry sits completely inside it, and you get the total of the cells those entries cover. Do the same with the down clues. If the across entries and down entries cover exactly the same cells, the two totals match and you’ve learned nothing. If one side covers one extra cell, the difference between the totals is that cell.

Killer Sudoku players call the extra cell an innie or an outie, and Wikipedia’s Killer Sudoku article gives the 45-based formulas. In Kakuro you don’t need 45 at all. You compare across against down.

Calculating an “Outie”

An outie is a cell outside your region that gets dragged into the count because one of your entries runs past the edge. Here’s the grid this article will solve. Clue cells read down\across: 8\ is a down clue of 8, and \19 is an across clue of 19.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 11\   | 12\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |   ·   |   ·   |   ·   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \19 |   ·   |   ·   |   ·   | 10\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \18 | OUTIE |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \11 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The dotted cells form a 2×3 block. The across clues 10 and 19 cover it exactly: 10 + 19 = 29. The down clues 11, 12, and 8 also cover it, but the 8 runs one cell further down. So 11 + 12 + 8 = 31 counts the block plus that cell.

Outie = (clues that run outside) − (clues that fit inside) = 31 − 29 = 2.

Calculating an “Innie”

An innie is the reverse: a cell inside your region that one direction counts and the other doesn’t, because its entry in that direction leaves the region.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 11\   | 12\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \19 |       |       |       | 10\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \18 | INNIE |   ·   |   ·   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \11 |   ·   |   ·   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Take the bottom-right tail as your region. The across clues 18 and 11 cover all five cells: 29. The down clues 10 and 17 cover the four dotted cells but miss the innie, whose down entry (the 8) climbs out of the region. They total 27.

Innie = (clues covering the whole region) − (clues covering all but the innie) = 29 − 27 = 2.

Same cell, same answer, from opposite sides. It was an outie of the top block and an innie of the tail. You’ll find it either way, so start from whichever region is easier to add up.

Advanced Multi-Block Counting

Combining Regions

Killer Sudoku extends the rule to two regions (90) and three (135). Kakuro doesn’t need multiples because you never compare against a fixed number. Any region works as long as every entry you count lies completely inside it. That means irregular shapes are fine: L-shapes, staircases, a block plus a tail.

Two habits make bigger regions manageable:

  • Subtract known cells as you go. If the leftover is two cells but one is already solved, take its digit off the difference and you’re back to a single cell.
  • Treat a two-cell leftover as a new clue. If the totals differ by 17 and the leftover is two cells, you’ve just created a hidden “17 in two”, which is {8, 9}. Write it in the margin. It behaves exactly like a printed clue.

A nine-cell entry inside the region always counts as 45, which is the one spot where the literal number still shows up in this kind of count.

Practical Example: Cracking the Block

Here’s the full grid, blank:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 11\   | 12\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \19 |       |       |       | 10\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \18 |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \11 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

It looks friendly, but it isn’t. The only magic block is the 17 down, and it only tells you that its two cells are 8 and 9 in some order. Every other clue has at least two workable sets, and none of the crossings narrow them to one. Clue-by-clue logic stalls before it places a single digit.

Step 1: Add the across clues of the top block. 10 + 19 = 29.

Step 2: Add the down clues that touch it. 11 + 12 + 8 = 31.

Step 3: Take the difference. 31 − 29 = 2. The cell under the block, at the bottom of the 8 down, is a 2.

One digit turns the whole grid over:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 11\   | 12\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |       |       |  1 5  |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \19 |       |       |  1 5  | 10\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \18 |   2   |  7 9  |  7 9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \11 |       |  8 9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
  • The 18 across now needs 16 from its last two cells. That’s {7, 9}, a magic block that didn’t exist a minute ago. Its right-hand cell is also in the 17 down {8, 9}, so it’s 9. The other cell is 7.
  • The 10 down gets 7 on top, so 3 below it. The 11 across gets that 3 and needs 8 beside it, which completes the 17 down as 9 + 8.
  • The 8 down has 6 left for its top two cells: {1, 5} or {2, 4}. The 2 is already used in that entry, so it’s {1, 5}.
  • The 19 across has no three-cell set containing a 1 (the best you can do is 1 + 9 + 8 = 18), so its right-hand cell is 5 and the cell above is 1. The other two cells need 14, and the only way to make 14 alongside a 5 inside a 19 is {6, 8}.
  • The 12 down can’t be 6 + 6, so its bottom cell is 8 and its top is 4. That makes the 11 down 6 + 5, and the top row reads 5, 4, 1 = 10.
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 11\   | 12\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |   5   |   4   |   1   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \19 |   6   |   8   |   5   | 10\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \18 |   2   |   7   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \11 |   3   |   8   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Two sums and one subtraction solved a grid that combinations alone couldn’t start.

Best Practices and Tips

Do:

  • ✓ Reach for region counting when every clue around a block has too many combinations to pick from.
  • ✓ Look for regions that almost close: a block with one entry poking out, or a tail hanging off a block. The poke-out is your innie or outie.
  • ✓ Double-check your arithmetic. One slip and you’ll place a wrong digit with total confidence.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Assume an open block sums to 45. Only a nine-cell entry is guaranteed to.
  • ✗ Count an entry that’s only partly inside your region. Either it’s wholly inside or it stays out of the sum.
  • ✗ Start counting while magic blocks and easy crossings still give you moves. Setting up a count is slower than reading a 3 or a 17.

Speed tips:

  • Write the two totals in the margin next to the region. When you come back after solving elsewhere, you won’t have to add them up again.
  • Get comfortable with the habit on Killer Sudoku first. Its regions are fixed boxes, so you practice the counting without having to find the region.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

The calculated digit is 0, negative, or bigger than 9.

  • Cause: An arithmetic slip, an entry that sticks out of the region and got counted anyway, or a cell you forgot is covered twice.
  • Fix: List each entry you counted and check that every one of its cells is inside your boundary. Then add again.

The digit is between 1 and 9 but contradicts a pencil mark.

  • Cause: Usually the count is fine and the pencil mark is wrong. Sometimes the leftover is two cells and you counted it as one.
  • Fix: Recount the leftover cells. If there are two, you have their sum, not a single digit. Treat it as a new two-cell clue.

The totals match exactly.

  • Cause: Both directions cover the same cells, which is normal for a fully closed region.
  • Fix: Grow or shrink the region by one entry until one side covers a cell the other doesn’t.

Conclusion

Key takeaways:

  1. 1 through 9 sums to 45, but in Kakuro only a nine-cell entry is guaranteed to hold all of them.
  2. Long entries are short entries in disguise: the missing digits always sum to 45 minus the clue.
  3. Innies and outies come from counting one region across and down. The difference is the cell that only one direction covers.
  4. This breaks open sections that have no magic blocks to start from.

Next steps: In your next puzzle, find a block with exactly one entry poking out of it. Add the across clues, add the down clues, and subtract. If the result opens the block, you’ve got the habit.

title: Mastering the 45 Rule in Kakuro

content:
A fresh Kakuro grid sits in front of you, every white cell empty. Your eye lands on a 27 running across five cells, so you start there. 9, 8, 6, 3, 1? 9, 7, 5, 4, 2? 8, 7, 6, 4, 2? All valid. There are eleven different digit sets that add to 27 in five cells, and nothing yet tells you which one is right. You pencil in a few, erase them, and start to wonder whether everyone else is just better at math.

They aren’t. They started somewhere else. In the corner of that same grid sits a little 4 over two cells, and that clue has exactly one answer. Kakuro solvers call these unique sums, and you should find every one of them before you touch anything else.

Understanding Unique Sums

The Math Behind the Magic

Two rules create unique sums: you can only use digits 1 through 9, and no digit can repeat within an entry. Together, those rules squeeze the extreme ends of the number range.

Take two cells. The smallest sum you can make is 1 + 2 = 3. The largest is 9 + 8 = 17. Near those edges you have almost no room to move. A clue of 3 has only one candidate pair. So does 17. Move one step toward the middle and the options open up. A 5 can be 1 + 4 or 2 + 3. A 10 can be 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, or 4 + 6.

That’s the whole idea. Clues near the bottom or top of what an entry can hold have one valid set of digits. Clues in the middle have several. Start at the edges, and you start with facts instead of possibilities.

Conceptis Puzzles calls an entry like this a “magic block”: a run of cells whose digits are fixed the moment you know its length and its sum. The name fits. Each one hands you its digits for free.

The Lows: 3 and 4

3 in two cells = {1, 2}. List every pair of digits that adds to 3: 1 + 2. That’s the only one. There’s no 0, so nothing else fits.

4 in two cells = {1, 3}. List every pair that adds to 4: 1 + 3 and 2 + 2. The no-repeat rule kills 2 + 2, which leaves 1 + 3.

+-------+-------+-------+       +-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |  1 2  |  1 2  |       |   \4  |  1 3  |  1 3  |
+-------+-------+-------+       +-------+-------+-------+

You know both digits the moment you see the clue. You don’t know which cell holds which digit, so both cells get both pencil marks.

The Highs: 16 and 17

17 in two cells = {8, 9}. The only pair that reaches 17 is 9 + 8. Nothing else gets that high.

16 in two cells = {7, 9}. The candidates are 9 + 7 and 8 + 8. The repeat rule kills 8 + 8, so it’s 7 and 9.

+-------+-------+-------+       +-------+-------+-------+
|   \16 |  7 9  |  7 9  |       |   \17 |  8 9  |  8 9  |
+-------+-------+-------+       +-------+-------+-------+

The Mirror Principle

Mapping the low anchors to their high twins:

graph LR
    A[Low Anchor: 3] -->|"{1, 2}"| C{Mirror Formula: 10 - X}
    C -->|"{9, 8}"| D[High Anchor: 17]
    B[Low Anchor: 4] -->|"{1, 3}"| C
    C -->|"{9, 7}"| E[High Anchor: 16]

Notice the mirror. The high pairs are the low pairs flipped around 10: 1 becomes 9, 2 becomes 8, 3 becomes 7. So {1,2} for 3 mirrors to {9,8} for 17, and {1,3} for 4 mirrors to {9,7} for 16. Memorize two pairs and you get the other two free.

The same pattern holds for longer entries. Three cells have their own four unique sums (6, 7, 23, and 24), and so do four cells (10, 11, 29, and 30). Start with the two-cell set. Two-cell entries are everywhere on beginner grids, and four pairs are easy to hold in your head.

Practical Example: Finding the Anchors

Here’s a full beginner grid. Clue cells read down\across: 3\ is a down clue of 3, \4 is an across clue of 4, and 24\16 holds a down 24 and an across 16.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 25\   |#######| 24\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |       |       | 24\16 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \25 |       |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\19 |       |       |       |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |       |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |       |       |   \4  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Fourteen clues. Don’t do any arithmetic yet. Just scan.

Step 1: Scan for 3s and 4s over two cells. You’ll find four: the across 4 in the top-left, the down 3 above the first column, the across 4 in the bottom row, and the down 3 on the right edge.

Step 2: Pencil in their pairs. {1,2} for each 3, {1,3} for each 4.

Step 3: Scan for 16s and 17s over two cells. Four more: the across 16 and down 17 in the top-right, and the across 17 and down 16 in the bottom-left.

Step 4: Pencil in their pairs. {7,9} for each 16, {8,9} for each 17.

Bonus scan: three-cell anchors. The 24\16 cell’s down clue covers three cells. 24 in three cells is unique: {7,8,9}.

Mark the four corner cells with a star for now. Each one sits inside two anchors at once, and you’ll come back to them in a moment.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 25\   |#######| 24\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   *   |  1 3  | 24\16 |  7 9  |   *   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \25 |  1 2  |       | 7 8 9 |       |  8 9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\19 |       | 7 8 9 |       |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |  7 9  |       | 7 8 9 |       |  1 2  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   *   |  8 9  |   \4  |  1 3  |   *   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Nine anchors, fifteen cells narrowed down, and you haven’t made a single decision. That’s the foothold.

The starred cells are where it pays off. Take the top-left one. The across 4 says it’s 1 or 3. The down 3 says it’s 1 or 2. Only 1 satisfies both, so it’s a 1. The rest of each pair follows: the across 4 needs a 3 beside it, and the down 3 needs a 2 below it.

The other three corners work the same way:

  • Top-right: across 16 {7,9} meets down 17 {8,9}. The only shared digit is 9.
  • Bottom-left: across 17 {8,9} meets down 16 {7,9}. Again, 9.
  • Bottom-right: across 4 {1,3} meets down 3 {1,2}. It’s 1.
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 25\   |#######| 24\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   1   |   3   | 24\16 |   7   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \25 |   2   |       | 7 8 9 |       |   8   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\19 |       | 7 8 9 |       |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   7   |       | 7 8 9 |       |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   8   |   \4  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Twelve cells solved, with nothing harder than “which digit appears in both lists?” That move has a name, cross-referencing, and it gets its own article next in this series.

The middle nine cells take more work, but the corners give you plenty to start from. Row 2 already has a 2 and an 8, so its middle three cells must sum to 25 − 10 = 15. Try finishing the grid yourself. The answer key is at the end of this article.

Do’s and Don’ts

Do:

  • ✓ Memorize 3 = {1,2}, 4 = {1,3}, 16 = {7,9}, and 17 = {8,9} today. It takes five minutes and pays off on every grid you’ll ever solve.
  • ✓ Pencil both digits into both cells when you don’t know the order yet.
  • ✓ Run the full anchor scan before you commit to any digit.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Assume you know the order. Knowing an entry is {1,3} doesn’t tell you which cell holds the 1. The crossing clue decides that.
  • ✗ Mistake near-misses for unique sums. A 5 in two cells looks small enough, but it has two answers: {1,4} and {2,3}.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

“I found a 4, but it crosses a 20 across four cells. Neither 1 nor 3 helps.” You’ve hit a wide-open intersection. A 20 in four cells has twelve possible digit sets, and plenty of them contain a 1 or a 3, so the crossing tells you nothing yet. Leave the {1,3} pencil marks in place and move to a different anchor. As you fill in other cells along that 20, its options shrink, and eventually one of them will force the 1 or the 3 into place.

“I memorized the pairs but keep mixing up 16 and 17.” Use the mirror. 17 is the flip of 3 ({1,2} → {9,8}), and 16 is the flip of 4 ({1,3} → {9,7}). Or check the arithmetic directly: if your pair for 16 includes an 8, the other digit would have to be another 8, which is illegal.

Conclusion

Unique sums turn a wall of clues into a handful of known starting points. They’re the reason experienced solvers never start in the middle of the grid.

Key takeaways:

  1. A unique sum has only one valid set of digits for its entry length.
  2. For two-cell entries: 3 = {1,2}, 4 = {1,3}, 16 = {7,9}, 17 = {8,9}.
  3. These anchors are where every solve starts, and where they cross each other, you often get a definite digit right away.

Next steps: Knowing the digits is half the job. To learn which cell gets which digit, especially away from the corners, read the next article in the series.

You see SCARLET, MUSTARD, PLUM and BLUE, and you’re already reaching for the Submit button. Four colours, done. Except PEACOCK is sitting two tiles over, smirking. Now you have five candidates for four slots, one mistake on the board, and a creeping suspicion that this puzzle was written by someone who enjoys watching you squirm. It was.

The rules are short. Sixteen words hide four groups of four. Pick four you think belong together and submit. Find all four groups before you make four mistakes.

The board

Loading puzzle...

How to play

  • Tap four tiles to select them, then Submit. Tap a selected tile again to drop it.
  • A correct guess collapses into a coloured banner. Yellow groups are the most direct; purple groups are the most devious.
  • A wrong guess costs one of your four mistakes. If three of your four picks belong together, you’ll see One away…
  • Repeating a guess you’ve already tried is free, so experiment with combinations.
  • Shuffle rearranges the tiles when your eyes start seeing the same false pattern. Name a Group reveals one group’s title, easiest first.

Stuck?

  1. Count the candidates. If five words fit a group, one of them belongs somewhere else. Work out which group could use the spare before you submit.
  2. Read words as parts of other words. Purple groups rarely mean the obvious thing. Try putting something in front of each word, or after it.
  3. Solve from the edges. Lock in the group you’re surest of first. Every solved group removes four tiles of noise.

Your progress saves on this device, including which groups you’ve found and how many mistakes you have left.

content:
The cover says “Extreme Kakuro.” You open to a 15x15 grid and finish it in twelve minutes, because every corner has a 3 or a 17 in two cells that practically fills itself in. Two pages later there’s a little 7x7 marked “Medium.” Forty minutes in, you’re staring at a block of empty cells with no idea where to start.

The labels aren’t lying on purpose. They’re measuring the wrong thing. Big grids take longer; they aren’t necessarily harder. What makes a Kakuro hard is the toughest step the solver is forced to make, and that’s something you choose when you build the puzzle. This article sets out a four-tier grading scale, shows what each level looks like on the page, grades the series 7x7 grid, and then refills the same layout so it needs a deduction one tier harder.

Grid Size vs. Difficulty

Long Isn’t Hard

A 15x15 grid full of easy steps is a lot of easy steps. It takes time, not thought. A 7x7 can force a step that takes real insight, and one such step is enough to make the whole puzzle hard.

So define difficulty this way: the hardest technique the solver must use to finish without guessing. Not the average step, and not the number of steps. The single hardest one.

Inconsistent Labels

It’s tempting to label puzzles by grid size or clue count, because those are easy to measure. The result is a set of puzzles where “Hard” means three different things on three pages. Solvers notice. Grading by technique fixes that, because every label means the same deduction wherever it appears.

A Four-Tier Grading Scale

This is a practical scale for constructors, not an industry standard. Each tier is a kind of deduction, and a puzzle’s grade is the highest tier it requires.

Tier 1: Magic Blocks (Easy)

Some sums have only one possible set of digits. These magic blocks let the solver read digits almost straight off the clue:

Run length Magic blocks
2 cells 3 {1,2}, 4 {1,3}, 16 {7,9}, 17 {8,9}
3 cells 6 {1,2,3}, 7 {1,2,4}, 23 {6,8,9}, 24 {7,8,9}
4 cells 10 {1,2,3,4}, 11 {1,2,3,5}, 29 {5,7,8,9}, 30 {6,7,8,9}

When two magic blocks cross, the shared cell often falls out immediately. A 17 across ({8, 9}) crossing a 16 down ({7, 9}) shares only 9, so that cell is 9.

Not every pair can cross. A 3 in two cells is {1, 2}, and it shares nothing with a 16 or a 17. Put them across each other and the shared cell has no possible digit. That isn’t a hard puzzle; it’s a broken one.

Tier 2: Intersections (Medium)

Most clues have several possible sets. The solver narrows a cell by comparing what its across run allows with what its down run allows, then keeps comparing as digits fill in. That takes pencil marks and attention, but no new ideas.

The series grid’s first move is a Tier 2 step. The 6 down along the right edge is three cells, so it’s {1, 2, 3}, a magic block. The 27 across along the bottom row is four cells, which could be {3, 7, 8, 9}, {4, 6, 8, 9} or {5, 6, 7, 9}. Only 3 appears in both, so the corner cell r6c6 is 3. One magic block, one comparison.

Intersection Logic covers this tier in depth from the solver’s side.

Tier 3: Region Counts, Innies and Outies (Hard)

Pick a block of cells. Add up the across clues that cover it exactly, then add up the down clues that pass through it. If the down runs stick out past the block, or don’t fully cover it, the difference between the two totals is the value of the cells that only one direction covers. Those cells are outies (outside the block) or innies (inside it).

No 45 is involved. In Kakuro you compare across against down. The number 45 only enters the count when a run is all nine cells long, because only a nine-cell run is guaranteed to hold 1 through 9. Mastering the 45 Rule covers the solving side.

Tier 4: Parity and Chains (Expert)

Odd/even counting across connected runs, and short “if this cell is 4, then that one can’t be 2” chains. This is the top of the scale. Anything beyond it requires guessing, and a good puzzle never does. Eliminating Guesswork in Kakuro works through examples.

The grading rule: Tier 1 → Easy, Tier 2 → Medium, Tier 3 → Hard, Tier 4 → Expert.

As a test you run on your own grid, the scale works as a ladder. Stop at the first rung that finishes the puzzle:

What Each Level Looks Like

Easy

Several magic blocks spread around the grid, usually near corners and edges. Each placed digit leads straight to the next one, and the solver rarely needs to hold more than one run in their head.

Medium

A few magic blocks, plus clues with several possible sets. The solver needs intersections and some pencil marks, but never has to step back and count a whole region.

The series grid, as repaired in How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution, is a Medium:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |       |       |       |       | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |       |       | 19\8  |       |       |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |       |       | 17\8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

It has three magic blocks: the 3 across in row 3 ({1, 2}), the 17 down in column 4 ({8, 9}) and the 6 down in column 6 ({1, 2, 3}). Intersections finish every cell from there. No region counts, no parity.

Hard

Few magic blocks, and the easy steps run out partway through. The solver gets a foothold, makes some progress, then hits a wall that only a region count gets past.

A common misconception is that a Hard grid must have no magic blocks at all, or that the first digit should need a region count. That usually makes a puzzle nobody can get into. The more satisfying shape is the one in the next section: a few footholds, then a wall.

Pacing the Solve

A good hard puzzle has a shape: foothold → wall → breakthrough → cascade.

The foothold gets the solver onto the page and building momentum. The wall is where the difficulty lives: progress stops, and the usual moves don’t work. The breakthrough is the one deduction that gets past it. The cascade is the reward, as the rest of the grid falls quickly once the wall is down.

One clear wall feels better than several small ones. Three stalls in a row reads as a slog, not a challenge. And after the breakthrough, the finish should be fast. A second wall right after the first one makes the breakthrough feel like it didn’t count.

Compare the two series grids. The Medium never stalls. Every move leads to the next at a steady rate. The Hard, below, places seven cells, stops dead with 17 cells open, and then finishes all 16 remaining cells after one region count. Same layout, a different shape entirely.

Practical Example: Making the Series Grid Harder

The goal: keep the series layout and make it need a Tier 3 step.

  • Same layout, so same symmetry
  • One magic block only
  • Intersections alone must stall
  • A region count must restart the solve
  • Still exactly one solution

Step 1: Grade the starting grid. The Main grid above solves on Tiers 1 and 2, so it’s Medium.

Step 2: Refill the layout. Changing a few clues on the Main grid isn’t enough, because a clue is just the sum of the digits under it. To change what the solver experiences, you change the digits. Here’s the same layout with a completely new fill:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 24\   | 15\   |  6\   | 14\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \13 |       |       |       |       | 24\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |       |       | 11\12 |       |       |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \10 |       |       |  7\5  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \14 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Only one clue is a magic block now: the 24 down in column 1, which must be {7, 8, 9}.

Step 3: Solve until it stalls. The 24 gives the first foothold. r2c1 is also in the 13 across on row 2, a four-cell run. Four different digits adding to 13 can’t include anything above 7 (13 − 1 − 2 − 3), so r2c1 = 7. Six more cells fall, mostly on the right side: r6c5 = 9, r5c5 = 8, r3c4 = 9, r3c5 = 3, r4c5 = 4 and r4c6 = 1.

Then nothing. Seventeen cells are still open, each with two or three candidates, and no crossing narrows any of them further.

Step 4: Count the region. Take the block covered by the three left-hand across runs: row 1 (17), row 2 (13) and the left run of row 3 (12). Across total: 42.

Now add the down runs that pass through that block: column 1 (24), column 2 (15), the top run of column 3 (6) and the top run of column 4 (14). Down total: 59.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 24\   | 15\   |  6\   | 14\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   ·   |   ·   |   ·   |   ·   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \13 |   7   |   ·   |   ·   |   ·   | 24\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |   ·   |   ·   | 11\12 | 9 OUT |   3   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \10 | OUTIE |       |  7\5  |   4   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \14 |       |       |   8   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |       |       |   9   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The down runs cover the whole block plus two cells that poke out of it: r4c2 (the bottom of the column-2 run) and r3c4 (the bottom of the column-4 run). So those two cells must add up to the difference: 59 − 42 = 17. Two cells making 17 can only be 8 and 9. r3c4 is already 9, so r4c2 = 8.

Step 5: Watch the cascade. With r4c2 = 8, the 10 across on row 4 makes r4c3 = 2. From there the remaining cells fall in a steady run: r3c2, r5c3, r6c3, r2c4, r3c1, r6c4, r6c6, r1c1, r1c4, r5c4, r5c6, r1c2, r1c3, r2c2 and r2c3. That’s 16 cells after the breakthrough, no second wall.

Step 6: Confirm one solution. A forced-only solve that includes the region count completes, and a solution counter (see Build a Kakuro Solver and Generator in Python) finds exactly one answer.

You end up with the same layout and a Hard grade: one clear wall, then a fast finish. Both grids are in the printable series puzzles. Solve them back to back and you’ll feel exactly where the Hard one stops you.

Best Practices

Do:

  • ✓ Grade by test-solving and noting the hardest step you needed.
  • ✓ Keep difficulty consistent across a set of puzzles.
  • ✓ Give hard puzzles one clear breakthrough rather than many small stalls.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Confuse a puzzle with two solutions with a hard puzzle. Ambiguous is not difficult.
  • ✗ Require guessing at any level.
  • ✗ Grade by grid size.

Troubleshooting

A “Hard” puzzle solves too fast. A magic block or a crossing that allows only one digit gives the solver a way around the wall. Find the shortcut in your test solve, change the digits there so its clue has more possible sets, and re-check that the puzzle still has exactly one solution.

Testers give up on an “Expert” puzzle. The breakthrough is too well hidden, or there are several walls in a row. Make the key region easier to spot: a block with only one or two cells poking out is much easier to find than one spread across the grid. Or add a foothold near it so the solver’s attention is already in the right place.

The region count gives an impossible number. A run you counted doesn’t lie completely inside or completely across the region, or you counted a clue twice. List every run you’re counting, mark which cells each one covers, and check that the across runs cover the block exactly.

What to Take Away

Difficulty is the hardest step you force, not the size of the grid. Grade on four tiers: magic blocks, intersections, region counts, parity and chains. Region counts compare across with down, and 45 doesn’t come into it. The best hard puzzles give a foothold, one wall and a fast finish. And to make a grid harder, change its digits, not just its label.

content:
You’ve spotted the 16 in the corner of a Kakuro grid. Two cells, so it’s 7 and 9. You pencil “7 9” into both cells and feel good about it for about four seconds. Then you notice the 17 next to it is “8 9” in both cells too, and the 24 below is “7 8 9” in all three, and the top corner of the grid now looks like a phone keypad.

Knowing the combination is half the job. The other half is knowing which digit goes in which cell, and the clue itself can’t tell you that. The clue running the other way through the same cell can. Every white cell sits in exactly one across entry and one down entry, and the digit in it has to satisfy both. Read the two together and most of those pencil marks never need to be written.

The Power of Opposites

High Meets Low

Every entry has a ceiling and a floor, set by its clue and its length:

  • Highest possible digit = clue − (the smallest digits that could fill the other cells)
  • Lowest possible digit = clue − (the largest digits that could fill the other cells)

A 14 in four cells has a ceiling of 14 − (1 + 2 + 3) = 8. A 23 in three cells has a floor of 23 − (9 + 8) = 6.

Now cross a high clue with a low one:

17 across (2 cells):   {8, 9}
14 down   (4 cells):   ceiling = 14 − (1 + 2 + 3) = 8
Shared cell:           {8, 9} ∩ {1 … 8} = 8

The 9 can’t go in the shared cell because the 14 can’t hold a 9 anywhere. So the shared cell is 8, the 17’s other cell is 9, and the 14 down has also been decided: the only four-cell set for 14 that contains an 8 is {1, 2, 3, 8}. One glance placed two digits and settled a clue with five possible sets.

Push the gap further and the intersection vanishes. A 16 in two cells {7, 9} crossing a 10 in four cells {1, 2, 3, 4} has no digit in common. A valid puzzle will never contain that crossing. If you think you see one, recount the cells, because one of the clues isn’t what you think it is.

Low Meets Low

Two small clues crossing each other work just as fast, because they compete for the same few digits. A 3 in two cells is {1, 2}. A 4 in two cells is {1, 3}. Where they cross, the only digit both allow is 1.

The high end mirrors it: 16 {7, 9} crossing 17 {8, 9} shares only 9. Both appear constantly in grid corners, where an across entry and a down entry start from the same clue cell.

Eliminating Candidates

Most crossings won’t hand you a single digit. They’ll trim a list, and trimming adds up.

The “Too Big” Rule

If a low clue crosses a looser one, the low clue’s ceiling caps the shared cell. Take a 10 in two cells, which could be {1, 9}, {2, 8}, {3, 7}, or {4, 6}. Cross it with a 6 in three cells, which is {1, 2, 3}. The shared cell can’t be bigger than 3, so it takes the small half of a pair (1, 2, or 3) and the 10’s other cell takes the matching big half (9, 8, or 7). The {4, 6} pair is gone, and the other cell has lost every candidate below 7.

The “Too Small” Rule

The reverse is easier to miss. A big digit in a modest entry eats the budget for every other cell in it. If the remaining cells can’t reach their own minimums, the big digit doesn’t fit.

Say a 17 runs down four cells, and the bottom cell can only be 6 or 7. Try a 9 at the top. The middle two cells would need to total 17 − 9 − 6 = 2 at most, and two different digits can’t add up to less than 1 + 2 = 3. So the top cell is not 9. That’s the exact move the practical example below needs.

Common Intersection Cheat Sheet

These crossings show up in almost every grid. Learn the first block and you’ll place digits in corners without thinking.

Across Down Shared cell Notes
3 {1,2} 4 {1,3} 1 Forced
4 {1,3} 7-in-3 {1,2,4} 1 Forced
17 {8,9} 16 {7,9} 9 Forced
16 {7,9} 23-in-3 {6,8,9} 9 Forced
3 {1,2} 6-in-3 {1,2,3} 1 or 2 Needs a third clue
4 {1,3} 6-in-3 {1,2,3} 1 or 3 Needs a third clue
17 {8,9} 24-in-3 {7,8,9} 8 or 9 Needs a third clue
16 {7,9} 24-in-3 {7,8,9} 7 or 9 Needs a third clue
4 {1,3} 16 {7,9} none Can’t appear in a valid puzzle

The table works in both directions. Swap across and down and the answers stay the same.

High Sum vs. Moderate Sum

Moderate clues don’t force digits, but magic blocks still trim them. A 16 {7, 9} crossing a 12 in two cells, which could be {3, 9}, {4, 8}, or {5, 7}:

  • 9 in the shared cell works, paired with 3.
  • 7 in the shared cell works, paired with 5.
  • The {4, 8} pair has nothing to offer the 16, so it’s gone.

The 12’s other cell drops from six candidates to two: {3, 5}.

Practical Example: Forcing a Corner

Here’s a grid with a corner where a 17 across meets a 24 down. Clue cells read down\across.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######| 24\   | 16\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  7\17 |       |       |#######| 17\   | 21\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |       |       |       |   \16 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \9  |       |       |#######|  3\8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \9  |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \8  |       |       |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 1: Compare the candidate lists. The 17 across is {8, 9}. The 24 down is {7, 8, 9}. The corner cell sits in both, so it’s 8 or 9. The 7 is out.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######| 24\   | 16\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  7\17 |  8 9  |  8 9  |#######| 17\   | 21\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |       | 7 8 9 |  7 9  |   \16 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \9  |       | 7 8 9 |#######|  3\8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 2: Use the neighbor. The 17’s other cell sits on top of the 16 down, which is {7, 9}. {8, 9} against {7, 9} leaves only 9. So the 17 reads 8, 9, and the corner is 8.

Step 3: Let it cascade. The 16 down has 9 on top, so 7 below. The 24 down still needs a 7 and a 9 for its last two cells. The middle cell sits in the 21 across, which already has that 7, so it takes the 9 and the bottom cell takes the 7. The 9 across now needs 2 beside that 7, and the 7 down needs 5 above the 2. Check the 21 across: 5 + 9 + 7 = 21.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######| 24\   | 16\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  7\17 |   8   |   9   |#######| 17\   | 21\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |   5   |   9   |   7   |   \16 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \9  |   2   |   7   |#######|  3\8  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 4: The right side needs the “too small” rule. The 16 across is {7, 9}. The 3 down is {1, 2}, so the 8 across at the bottom has 7 or 6 beside it. Now look at the 17 running down four cells:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |   5   |   9   |   7   |   \16 |  7 9  |  7 9  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \9  |   2   |   7   |#######|  3\8  |   ?   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \9  |  1 2  |   ?   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \8  |  1 2  |  6 7  |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

If its top cell were 9, the two ? cells would need 17 − 9 − 6 = 2 or less. Impossible. So the top is 7, which makes its neighbor 9. The bottom can no longer be 7, so it’s 6, which puts 2 beside it and 1 above that. The two ? cells now total 17 − 7 − 6 = 4, so they’re {1, 3}. The 9 across already has a 1, so its ? is 3 and its last cell is 5. The upper ? is 1, and the 8 across finishes with 7. The 21 down checks out: 9 + 7 + 5 = 21.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######| 24\   | 16\   |#######|#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  7\17 |   8   |   9   |#######| 17\   | 21\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \21 |   5   |   9   |   7   |   \16 |   7   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \9  |   2   |   7   |#######|  3\8  |   1   |   7   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \9  |   1   |   3   |   5   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \8  |   2   |   6   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

No guesses, and the only arithmetic harder than the clues themselves was one subtraction.

Best Practices and Tips

Do:

  • ✓ Read the crossing entry before writing any candidates in a cell.
  • ✓ Hunt for clashes between a high clue and a low one. Those are the fastest eliminations on the board.
  • ✓ Work out the ceiling and floor of a long entry once and write them by the clue.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Write out every candidate for a 20 in five cells before checking what its crossings allow. That clue has six possible sets, and most cells will drop to two or three candidates as soon as you look across.
  • ✗ Trust a pencil mark that was written before its crossing entry changed. Re-check it.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

A shared cell has no candidates left.

  • Cause: Usually a miscounted entry length. A 16 in two cells is {7, 9}. A 16 in three cells has eight possible sets.
  • Fix: Recount both entries, then recompute their ceilings and floors.

A candidate you allowed breaks the entry later.

  • Cause: You worked out the ceiling from the clue alone and ignored a digit already placed in the entry. If a 4 already sits in a four-cell 14, the other three cells share 10 and can’t use another 4, so their ceiling is 10 − (1 + 2) = 7, not 8.
  • Fix: Subtract placed digits first, then work out the ceiling from what’s left.

Two candidates survive every crossing.

  • Cause: Intersections alone can’t settle that cell.
  • Fix: Move on and come back. If the whole grid stalls, try the 45 rule or the deductions in Eliminating Guesswork.

Conclusion

Key takeaways:

  1. Every cell answers to two clues. The digit has to fit both.
  2. High-against-low and low-against-low crossings place digits on sight.
  3. Ceilings and floors (“too big” and “too small”) trim candidates even when nothing is forced.
  4. Cross-referencing is faster than listing full combinations, and it leaves fewer pencil marks to misread.

Next steps: Copy the cheat sheet table onto the back of your magic-block card. In your next puzzle, place every corner digit before writing a single pencil mark.

content:
You found the 3 in the corner of your Kakuro grid. Two cells, so it’s a 1 and a 2. You penciled both digits into both cells and felt good about it. Now you’re staring at those two cells, pencil hovering, and the question is simple: which one gets the 1?

You could flip a coin. Half the time you’d be right, and the other half you’d find out fifteen moves later, when a sum on the far side of the grid comes up one short. Knowing which digits belong in an entry is only half the work. The other half is knowing where each one goes, and the answer is almost never in the clue you’re staring at. It’s in the clue that crosses it.

The Power of the Intersection

The Dual-Constraint Rule

Every white cell in a Kakuro grid belongs to exactly two entries: one running across and one running down. Whatever digit you write there has to satisfy both clues at once.

In the diagrams below, clue cells read down\across: 3\ is a down clue of 3, \4 is an across clue of 4.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 12\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   ?   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

The ? cell answers to the \4 on its left, which needs two cells summing to 4, and to the 3\ above it, which needs two cells summing to 3. A digit that works for one clue and breaks the other is wrong, no matter how good it looks.

That’s the whole principle: the correct digit must appear in the candidate set of both entries. Write out what each clue allows, compare the two lists, and keep only what they share. The overlap is often a single digit.

Eliminating the Impossible

Cross-referencing works best when one of the two clues is a unique sum, or when a low clue crosses a high one.

Start with the low-meets-high case. A 4 over two cells crosses a 20 over three cells. The 4 can only be {1,3}. The 20 has four options: {3,8,9}, {4,7,9}, {5,6,9}, and {5,7,8}. Not one of them contains a 1, and only one contains a 3. The shared cell has to be 3, and the 20 has to be 3 + 8 + 9. One comparison gave you a digit and a full set of digits for the longer entry.

Now say a 16 over two cells crosses a 10 over two cells. The 16 can only be {7,9}. The 10 has four options: 1 + 9, 2 + 8, 3 + 7, or 4 + 6, so its cells could hold any of {1,2,3,4,6,7,8,9}. Compare the lists:

  • 16 allows: 7, 9
  • 10 allows: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9
  • Shared: 7, 9

That doesn’t force a digit yet, but it rules out six digits in that cell, and it tells you the 10 must be either 3 + 7 or 1 + 9. The 2 + 8 and 4 + 6 options are gone. One crossing cut the 10’s possibilities in half.

Push both clues to the extremes and the overlap disappears entirely. Picture a 16 over two cells crossing a 4 over two cells. The 16 needs {7,9}. The 4 needs {1,3}. They share nothing. No digit can satisfy both, so that layout can’t exist in a valid puzzle. If you ever see an empty overlap, you’ve misread a clue, miscounted an entry length, or made an error earlier. It’s an alarm, not a dead end.

Practical Example: The Corner Solve

Back to that corner, where a horizontal 4 meets a vertical 3. This time, solve all four cells.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 12\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

Intersection Logic Flow

Visualizing the cross-referencing process:

graph TD
    A[Horizontal Clue 4] -->|Requires| B("{1, 3}")
    C[Vertical Clue 3] -->|Requires| D("{1, 2}")
    B --> E{Intersection Cell}
    D --> E
    E -->|Must be shared| F["Candidate = 1"]

Step 1: List the horizontal 4. Two cells, sum of 4. Only {1,3} works.

Step 2: List the vertical 3. Two cells, sum of 3. Only {1,2} works.

Step 3: Find the intersection. The top-left white cell sits in both entries, so its digit must appear in {1,3} and {1,2}.

Step 4: Take the shared digit. The only digit in both sets is 1. The corner is 1.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 12\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   1   |  1 3  |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |  1 2  |       |
+-------+-------+-------+

Step 5: Fill the rest of each entry. The across 4 has one cell left: 4 − 1 = 3. The down 3 has one cell left: 3 − 1 = 2.

Now look at the bottom-right cell. Before the corner was solved, cross-referencing couldn’t help here. The across 11 allowed {2,9}, {3,8}, {4,7}, or {5,6}. The down 12 allowed {3,9}, {4,8}, or {5,7}. Their shared candidates were 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9, which is far too many to act on.

With the corner filled, both entries have one cell left. The across 11 already has a 2, so the last cell is 11 − 2 = 9. The down 12 already has a 3, so the last cell is 12 − 3 = 9. Both clues land on 9, which confirms it.

+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 12\   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   1   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |   2   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+

That last move is a forced digit. Once an entry has one empty cell, the digit isn’t a choice. It’s subtraction. And when the across and down subtractions agree, you get a free check on your work.

Cross-Referencing Away From the Corners

Corners are easy because both clues are unique sums. In the middle of the grid, one crossing usually narrows a cell without solving it, so you combine it with what the rest of the entry already knows.

Here’s the grid from The Magic of Unique Sums after its four corners are filled:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|  3\   | 25\   |#######| 24\   | 17\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \4  |   1   |   3   | 24\16 |   7   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \25 |   2   |       |   A   |       |   8   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\19 |       |       |       |  3\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   7   |       |       |       |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   8   |   \4  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Cell A sits in the down 24 that starts at the 24\16 cell. That entry covers three cells, so it has to be {7,8,9}. It also sits in the across 25, which already contains an 8. So A is 7 or 9. That’s as far as the crossing alone gets you.

Now list what the across 25 still needs. It has a 2 and an 8, so its three middle cells must add to 15 without using 2 or 8. Only three sets work: {1,5,9}, {3,5,7}, and {4,5,6}.

  • {4,5,6} has no 7 or 9, so it can’t fill A. Cross it out.
  • {3,5,7} needs a 3 somewhere in the middle. The cell left of A sits in the down 25, which already has a 3 at the top. The cell right of A sits in the other down 24, the five-cell one along the fifth column, which already has a 3 at the bottom. The 3 has nowhere to go. Cross it out.
  • {1,5,9} is all that’s left, and of those three digits only 9 fits A.

A = 9. Now A’s three-cell down 24 has 7 and 8 left for its other two cells. The bottom one sits in the across 27, which already has a 7, so it’s 8, and the middle one is 7. One deduction set off two more.

Do’s and Don’ts

Do:

  • ✓ Check the crossing clue every time before you write a final digit.
  • ✓ Hunt for places where a low unique sum crosses a high clue, like the 4 crossing the 20 above. Their overlap is often a single digit.
  • ✓ When a crossing narrows a cell to two digits, list the full combinations for the longer entry and test each one.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Forget to update the rest of both entries after you solve an intersection. The remaining sums just changed.
  • ✗ Validate a digit in one direction only. Every cell gets checked twice.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

“I cross-referenced two clues and they share no digits.” Something upstream is wrong. Either your list of combinations is incomplete, or an earlier digit is incorrect and has shrunk an entry’s options. Erase the pencil marks in both entries, recalculate each candidate set from the clue and the digits already placed, and compare again. If the overlap is still empty, trace back through the last few digits you placed in those entries.

“The two clues share three or four digits, so nothing is forced.” That’s normal for mid-range clues. Leave the pencil marks and work somewhere else. Each digit you place elsewhere removes candidates from these entries, and the overlap shrinks on its own.

Conclusion

Cross-referencing is what turns Kakuro from a stack of separate addition problems into one connected puzzle. Every digit you place sends information in two directions.

Key takeaways:

  1. Every white cell answers to two clues, one across and one down.
  2. The correct digit must appear in the candidate sets of both entries.
  3. Crossing two unique sums gives you your first definite digits. After that, subtraction and combination lists carry the solve into the middle of the grid.

Next steps: Practice on beginner grids by hunting for intersections where a unique sum crosses anything at all. Then read up on the habits that undo good logic.

The front door booms shut behind you and a bolt slides home on the far side. You didn’t hear anyone follow you up the drive. Somewhere down the hall is a dead man, a locked desk and three people who all have a very good reason to be somewhere else. The coachman is clear about it: nobody leaves until someone is named.

This is a narrative escape game, a little like a choose-your-own-adventure book that fights back. You read, you choose where to go, and when you hit a lock you have to work out the combination from what you’ve seen. Everything you need is somewhere in the house.

How to play

  • Locks take typed answers. Capitals, spaces and punctuation don’t matter, so 9:47 and 0947 count the same.

Stuck?

  1. Look before you fiddle. The foyer has two things worth examining before you go near a lock.
