content:
You write the obvious Kakuro solver first: try 1 through 9 in each empty cell, and back up whenever a sum goes wrong. The series 7x7 grid has 24 white cells. Trying every digit in every cell is 9²⁴ combinations, about 8 × 10²², and your laptop’s fan has opinions about that.

The fix isn’t a faster computer. It’s using what Kakuro already tells you. A clue of 6 over three cells doesn’t allow 729 possibilities. It allows exactly one set of digits, {1, 2, 3}, in some order. Build the solver around the sets each clue allows and the search shrinks to almost nothing.

A generator needs more than a solver, though. It has to prove there’s no second solution and say how hard the puzzle is. This article builds all three on one core, in plain Python with no dependencies, and tests them on the three versions of the series grid: Main (one solution, Medium), Draft (two solutions) and Hard (one solution, needs a region count).

Kakuro as a Search Problem

NP-Completeness in Plain Terms

Solving Kakuro in general is NP-complete. In practice, that means nobody knows a method that stays fast as grids grow without limit. Takahiro Seta showed it in a 2002 thesis, and Oliver Ruepp and Markus Holzer published a new proof in 2010.

It doesn’t mean your solver will be slow. Published grids are small, and every clue cuts the possibilities sharply. With the pruning below, the series grids solve in a few milliseconds. NP-completeness is a statement about the worst case on enormous grids, not about a 7x7 on your desk.

Cells, Candidates and Constraints

Frame the puzzle the way a constraint solver would:

  • Variables: each white cell.
  • Candidates: the digits each cell might still hold, starting at 1–9.
  • Constraints: each run’s digits add up to its clue, and no digit repeats within a run. Every cell belongs to one across run and one down run and has to satisfy both.

Everything below works by shrinking candidates until each cell has one left.

The Core Pieces

The code is one file, kakuro.py, shown in eight pieces. Paste them in order and you have the whole script. It needs Python 3.10 or later for int.bit_count() and nothing outside the standard library.

Combination Tables as Bitmasks

Store a set of digits as a 9-bit integer: bit 0 is digit 1, bit 8 is digit 9. The set {1, 2} is 0b000000011, and {1, 2, 3} is 0b000000111. Checking which digits two sets share is a single &.

Then precompute every digit set for every run length and total, using itertools.combinations. There are only 511 non-empty subsets of 1–9, so the whole table is tiny.

r"""kakuro.py: solve, count, grade and generate Kakuro puzzles.

Python 3.10+ (uses int.bit_count), standard library only.

Grid format: one line per row, cells separated by spaces.
  #      black cell with no clue
  .      white cell
  16\    clue cell: down 16
  \12    clue cell: across 12
  19\8   clue cell: down 19 and across 8
"""
import itertools
import random
import sys

FULL = 0b111111111  # candidates 1-9: bit k means digit k + 1


def bits(mask):
    """Yield each set bit of mask as its own one-bit mask."""
    while mask:
        low = mask & -mask
        yield low
        mask ^= low


def digit(bit):
    """Convert a one-bit mask back to its digit (0b100 -> 3)."""
    return bit.bit_length()


# COMBOS[(length, total)] -> every digit set (as a mask) that fills the run.
COMBOS = {}
for length in range(1, 10):
    for combo in itertools.combinations(range(1, 10), length):
        mask = sum(1 << (d - 1) for d in combo)
        COMBOS.setdefault((length, sum(combo)), []).append(mask)

COMBOS[(2, 3)] is [0b11], the single set {1, 2}. COMBOS[(4, 27)] holds three masks: {3, 7, 8, 9}, {4, 6, 8, 9} and {5, 6, 7, 9}.

Reading the Grid

Grids are plain text, one line per row, using the same down\across notation as the rest of this series. 16\ is a down clue of 16, \12 is an across clue of 12, 19\8 is both, # is an empty black cell and . is a white cell. Here’s the series Main grid as main.txt:

#    16\  12\  10\  8\   #    #
\12  .    .    .    .    #    #
\27  .    .    .    .    21\  #
\3   .    .    19\8 .    .    6\
#    \8   .    .    17\8 .    .
#    #    \16  .    .    .    .
#    #    \27  .    .    .    .

The parser walks every non-white cell and collects the white cells to its right and below. Each group becomes a run.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- parsing

def read_grid(text):
    """Return (cells, runs). Each run is (cells, total, name); total may be None."""
    rows = [line.split() for line in text.strip().splitlines()]
    runs = []
    for r, row in enumerate(rows):
        for c, tok in enumerate(row):
            if tok == ".":
                continue
            down, across = tok.split("\\") if "\\" in tok else ("", "")
            # An across run starts right of any black cell followed by white cells.
            cells = []
            cc = c + 1
            while cc < len(row) and row[cc] == ".":
                cells.append((r, cc))
                cc += 1
            if cells:
                runs.append((cells, int(across) if across else None, f"across r{r}c{c + 1}"))
            # A down run starts below any black cell followed by white cells.
            cells = []
            rr = r + 1
            while rr < len(rows) and rows[rr][c] == ".":
                cells.append((rr, c))
                rr += 1
            if cells:
                runs.append((cells, int(down) if down else None, f"down r{r + 1}c{c}"))
    whites = sorted({x for run_cells, _, _ in runs for x in run_cells})
    return whites, runs

A run whose total is None has no clue. That’s fine for a blank layout, which the generator uses later. For a puzzle, it means the grid is malformed, and the solver will report no solution.

Run-Level Filtering (the Step That Matters Most)

This is where Kakuro differs from a generic constraint solver. For each run:

  1. Keep only the digit sets that still fit. A set fits if its digits can go one per cell, with each digit inside that cell’s current candidates.
  2. Narrow each cell to the digits that appear in some surviving set, and that leave a valid placement for the rest of the run.

Repeat for every run until nothing changes. Because every cell sits in an across run and a down run, narrowing one run narrows its crossings on the next pass.

# ------------------------------------------------------- run-level filter

def fits(cells, mask, cand):
    """Can the digits in mask go one per cell, each within that cell's candidates?"""
    if not cells:
        return mask == 0
    first, rest = cells[0], cells[1:]
    for bit in bits(cand[first] & mask):
        if fits(rest, mask ^ bit, cand):
            return True
    return False


def propagate(cand, runs):
    """Narrow every cell to digits that appear in a still-possible set for its runs.

    Repeats until nothing changes. Returns False if some cell runs out of digits.
    """
    changed = True
    while changed:
        changed = False
        for cells, total, _ in runs:
            live = [m for m in COMBOS.get((len(cells), total), []) if fits(cells, m, cand)]
            for x in cells:
                others = [y for y in cells if y != x]
                allowed = 0
                for m in live:
                    for bit in bits(cand[x] & m & ~allowed):
                        if fits(others, m ^ bit, cand):
                            allowed |= bit
                if allowed != cand[x]:
                    if allowed == 0:
                        return False
                    cand[x] = allowed
                    changed = True
    return True


def is_solved(cand):
    return all(m.bit_count() == 1 for m in cand.values())

On the Main grid, the first thing this finds is r6c6 = 3. The 6 down along the right edge can only be {1, 2, 3}, the 27 across along the bottom can’t include 1 or 2, and 3 is the only digit left in their shared cell. Keep filtering and every cell on the Main grid resolves without a single guess. On the Hard grid it places 7 cells and stalls.

Plain forward checking, which only removes a placed digit from its neighbors, is much weaker. It doesn’t know that a 6 over three cells means {1, 2, 3}, so it can’t find r6c6 until it has guessed its way close. Run-level filtering does most of the solver’s work.

Backtracking with Fewest-Candidates-First

When filtering stalls, pick the open cell with the fewest candidates, try each one, filter again and recurse. Picking cells in reading order instead wastes time on cells that could still be almost anything. Copying the candidate dictionary before each trial makes undoing a failed branch free.

# ------------------------------------------------------------- searching

def solve(cand, runs, limit=2, found=None):
    """Collect up to `limit` solutions. Filter first, then branch on the tightest cell."""
    found = [] if found is None else found
    cand = dict(cand)
    if not propagate(cand, runs):
        return found
    open_cells = [x for x in cand if cand[x].bit_count() > 1]
    if not open_cells:
        found.append({x: digit(m) for x, m in cand.items()})
        return found
    x = min(open_cells, key=lambda y: cand[y].bit_count())  # fewest candidates first
    for bit in bits(cand[x]):
        if len(found) >= limit:
            break
        trial = dict(cand)
        trial[x] = bit
        solve(trial, runs, limit, found)
    return found


def count_solutions(cells, runs, limit=2):
    """0, 1, or `limit` (meaning "at least that many"). Stops as soon as it hits the limit."""
    return len(solve({x: FULL for x in cells}, runs, limit))

Note limit=2. To check uniqueness you don’t need every solution, just to know whether a second one exists. The moment the search finds two, it stops. A badly ambiguous grid can have hundreds of solutions, and counting them all would tell you nothing extra.

Grading by Simulating a Human

Solve time says nothing about difficulty. The computer finishes the Hard grid in about 3 milliseconds; a person might need half an hour. Instead, grade the way How to Set Kakuro Difficulty does: apply techniques in order and record the hardest one needed.

  • Pass A, run-level filtering, covers Tiers 1 and 2: magic blocks and intersections.
  • Pass B, region counts, covers Tier 3. Pick a set of runs in one direction, add their clues, then compare with the clues of the crossing runs. Cells that only one direction covers have a known total.
  • Anything left needs Tier 4 deductions (parity, chains) or guessing. Flag it for a human to look at.

Region counts compare across with down. Don’t hardcode 45; it only appears for a nine-cell run (see Mastering the 45 Rule).

# ------------------------------------------------------- region counting

def region_facts(runs, max_runs=3):
    """Across-vs-down counts: groups of 1-2 cells whose total the clues force.

    For a set of runs in one direction, add their clues (the region total). Every
    run in the other direction that touches the region either stays inside it or
    pokes out. Pokes-out cells are outies; region cells the inside runs miss are innies.
    """
    facts = []
    across = [r for r in runs if r[2].startswith("across")]
    down = [r for r in runs if r[2].startswith("down")]
    for first, second in ((across, down), (down, across)):
        for k in range(1, max_runs + 1):
            for group in itertools.combinations(first, k):
                region = {x for cells, _, _ in group for x in cells}
                region_total = sum(total for _, total, _ in group)
                touching = [r for r in second if region & set(r[0])]
                covered = {x for cells, _, _ in touching for x in cells}
                outies = covered - region
                if 1 <= len(outies) <= 2:
                    facts.append((sorted(outies), sum(t for _, t, _ in touching) - region_total))
                inside = [r for r in second if set(r[0]) <= region]
                innies = region - {x for cells, _, _ in inside for x in cells}
                if inside and 1 <= len(innies) <= 2:
                    facts.append((sorted(innies), region_total - sum(t for _, t, _ in inside)))
    return facts


def apply_region_facts(cand, runs, facts):
    """Place one cell from a region count if all other cells in its group are known."""
    for group, total in facts:
        unknown = [x for x in group if cand[x].bit_count() > 1]
        if len(unknown) != 1:
            continue
        known = sum(digit(cand[x]) for x in group if x not in unknown)
        value = total - known
        if 1 <= value <= 9 and cand[unknown[0]] & (1 << (value - 1)):
            cand[unknown[0]] = 1 << (value - 1)
            propagate(cand, runs)
            return True
    return False

On the Hard grid, one of these facts is the breakthrough from the difficulty article. The three left-hand across runs total 42, the four down runs through them total 59, and the two cells that poke out, r4c2 and r3c4, must add up to 17. Once r3c4 is known to be 9, apply_region_facts places r4c2 = 8, and filtering finishes the grid.

# ---------------------------------------------------------------- grading

def grade(text):
    cells, runs = read_grid(text)
    n = count_solutions(cells, runs)
    if n != 1:
        return f"rejected: {'no' if n == 0 else 'more than one'} solution"
    cand = {x: FULL for x in cells}
    propagate(cand, runs)                      # Pass A: magic blocks + intersections
    if is_solved(cand):
        return "Easy/Medium: run filtering solves it (Tiers 1-2)"
    facts = region_facts(runs)                 # Pass B: across-vs-down region counts
    while apply_region_facts(cand, runs, facts):
        if is_solved(cand):
            return "Hard: needs a region count (Tier 3)"
    return "Expert or guessing: needs parity, chains, or search (Tier 4+)"

Pass A lumps Easy and Medium together. If you want to split them, one approach is to count how many cells magic blocks alone can place before any intersection is needed. That’s left as an extension; the grader above doesn’t do it.

The Generator Pipeline

Here’s the whole pipeline before the details. Each box is a function from the script:

Step 1: Layout

Start with the clue border, then add interior black cells in symmetric pairs, (r, c) and (N − r, N − c). Reject any layout with a one-cell run, a white cell missing its across or down run, or disconnected white cells. Designing a Kakuro Grid covers the rules. The script below takes a finished layout as input, written with # and . only:

#    #    #    #    #    #    #
#    .    .    .    .    #    #
#    .    .    .    .    #    #
#    .    .    #    .    .    #
#    #    .    .    #    .    .
#    #    #    .    .    .    .
#    #    #    .    .    .    .

Steps 2–4: Fill, Count, Repair

Fill the white cells with random digits, no repeats within a run, and add up the clues. Then count solutions.

Here’s the uncomfortable part: random fills almost never have one solution. Using this script on the series layout, all 300 of 300 random fills had at least two solutions. Uniform random digits produce middle-sized sums with many possible sets, and the layout’s eight 2x2 white blocks leave plenty of room for swaps.

Throwing fills away and trying again doesn’t fix that. Repairing them does. Change one random digit (keeping runs repeat-free), recount, and keep the change if the solution count didn’t go up. In the same test, this reached a single solution in 13 of 20 attempts, at about 10 seconds per attempt on a laptop. It’s how the series grid was made: the Draft became the Main grid by changing one digit, r5c3 from 9 to 4. How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution shows why that change works.

# ------------------------------------------------------------- generating

def random_fill(cells, runs, rng, fixed=None):
    """Fill every white cell with 1-9, no repeats within a run, in random order.

    `fixed` maps cells to digits that must stay as given (e.g. a hidden answer).
    """
    runs_of = {x: [r[0] for r in runs if x in r[0]] for x in cells}
    fixed = fixed or {}
    fill = {}

    def place(i):
        if i == len(cells):
            return True
        x = cells[i]
        used = {fill[y] for run_cells in runs_of[x] for y in run_cells if y in fill}
        options = [d for d in range(1, 10) if d not in used]
        if x in fixed:
            options = [fixed[x]] if fixed[x] in options else []
        rng.shuffle(options)
        for d in options:
            fill[x] = d
            if place(i + 1):
                return True
            del fill[x]
        return False

    place(0)
    return fill


def with_totals(runs, fill):
    """Recalculate every clue from the current digits."""
    return [(cells, sum(fill[x] for x in cells), name) for cells, _, name in runs]


def repair(cells, runs, fill, rng, steps=400, limit=40, locked=()):
    """Change one digit at a time; keep the change if the solution count doesn't rise.

    Cells in `locked` are never changed.
    """
    runs_of = {x: [r[0] for r in runs if x in r[0]] for x in cells}
    changeable = [x for x in cells if x not in locked]
    score = count_solutions(cells, with_totals(runs, fill), limit)
    for _ in range(steps):
        if score == 1:
            break
        x = rng.choice(changeable)
        used = {fill[y] for run_cells in runs_of[x] for y in run_cells if y != x}
        options = [d for d in range(1, 10) if d not in used and d != fill[x]]
        if not options:
            continue
        old, fill[x] = fill[x], rng.choice(options)
        new_score = count_solutions(cells, with_totals(runs, fill), limit)
        if new_score <= score:
            score = new_score
        else:
            fill[x] = old
    return score == 1

repair counts up to 40 solutions rather than 2, so it can tell “slightly ambiguous” from “wildly ambiguous” and move toward fewer. Both functions also take an optional set of cells to leave alone: fixed in random_fill and locked in repair. That lets you build a grid around digits you’ve already chosen, like a hidden code (Designing Kakuro Grids That Hide an Answer uses it).

Step 5: Grade

Run grade() on the finished puzzle and file it under the right label, or send it back for another fill if you were aiming for a different tier.

Practical Implementation: Running It

The last piece prints solutions and makes the file runnable from the command line:

def show(cells, solution):
    rows = max(r for r, _ in cells) + 1
    cols = max(c for _, c in cells) + 1
    for r in range(rows):
        print(" ".join(str(solution.get((r, c), "#")) for c in range(cols)))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    for path in sys.argv[1:]:
        with open(path, encoding="utf-8") as f:
            text = f.read()
        cells, runs = read_grid(text)
        solutions = solve({x: FULL for x in cells}, runs, limit=2)
        print(f"{path}: {len(solutions)} solution(s) found (search stops at 2)")
        print(f"  grade: {grade(text)}")
        for s in solutions:
            show(cells, s)
            print()

To generate new puzzles, save the blank layout above as layout.txt and add a small driver, generate.py, next to kakuro.py:

"""generate.py: fill a layout, repair it until unique, print the puzzle and its grade."""
import random
import sys

from kakuro import grade, random_fill, read_grid, repair, with_totals


def to_text(layout_text, runs):
    """Write each run's total into its clue cell, in down\\across notation."""
    rows = [line.split() for line in layout_text.strip().splitlines()]
    clues = {}
    for cells, total, name in runs:
        r, c = cells[0]
        if name.startswith("across"):
            clues.setdefault((r, c - 1), ["", ""])[1] = str(total)
        else:
            clues.setdefault((r - 1, c), ["", ""])[0] = str(total)
    for (r, c), (down, across) in clues.items():
        rows[r][c] = down + "\\" + across
    return "\n".join(" ".join(f"{tok:<5}" for tok in row).rstrip() for row in rows)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open(sys.argv[1], encoding="utf-8") as f:
        layout = f.read()
    seed = int(sys.argv[2]) if len(sys.argv) > 2 else 1
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    cells, runs = read_grid(layout)

    for attempt in range(1, 11):
        fill = random_fill(cells, runs, rng)
        if repair(cells, runs, fill, rng):
            puzzle = to_text(layout, with_totals(runs, fill))
            print(f"unique after attempt {attempt}\n{puzzle}\ngrade: {grade(puzzle)}")
            break
    else:
        print("no unique puzzle in 10 attempts; try another seed or a layout with shorter runs")

Best Practices

Do:

  • ✓ Filter runs by digit set before every guess.
  • ✓ Stop counting at 2 solutions when checking uniqueness.
  • ✓ Grade with human-style passes, not timing.
  • ✓ Test your solver on a grid you know has two solutions, like draft.txt, not just ones that work.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Rely on forward checking alone.
  • ✗ Publish generated puzzles without a solution count.
  • ✗ Hardcode grid sizes. Nothing in this script assumes 7x7.

Troubleshooting

The generator never finds a unique fill. Uniform random digits produce mid-range sums with many possible sets, and large white areas leave room for swaps. Repair fills one digit at a time instead of starting over, and give repair more steps. If a layout still won’t settle, add black cells to shorten its longest runs.

The solver says a generated grid has no solution. The clue calculation and the solver disagree about which cells belong to a run. Build runs in one place, as read_grid does here, and use the same list for both calculating clues and solving.

Off-by-one digits everywhere. Mixing up bit positions and digits (digit 1 is bit 0, not bit 1) shifts every answer. Keep the conversion in one place, like digit() and the 1 << (d - 1) in the combination table, and never convert inline.

propagate is slow on big grids. fits tries placements recursively, which is fast for runs of up to five or six cells but grows quickly for long runs. For 15x15 grids with nine-cell runs, cache fits results per run between passes, or skip re-filtering runs whose cells haven’t changed.

What You’ve Built

Kakuro is NP-complete in general, but published grids solve in milliseconds with the right pruning. Combination tables plus run-level filtering do most of the work, and backtracking only has to cover what’s left. Count solutions and stop at two. Repair random fills one digit at a time instead of throwing them away. And grade by the hardest human technique needed, not by how long the computer took.

title: Build a Kakuro Solver and Generator in Python

content:
You’re down to the last four squares of an expert Kakuro. You try one fill and every clue checks out. You erase it, try the other, and every clue checks out again. Your pencil hovers. One of them has to be wrong, and the puzzle has stopped giving you hints.

So you pick one. If you’re lucky, the grid finishes and you feel nothing. If you’re not, you find out eleven moves later, and now you can’t tell which of those eleven moves to undo.

That’s bifurcation: picking a branch and seeing if it breaks. It’s the move pure-logic solvers try hardest to avoid, and on a well-built Kakuro you never need it. When two fills both seem to work, one of them breaks a rule you haven’t checked yet. The job is finding which rule, before you write anything down.

The Problem with Bifurcation

Why Guessing Ruins the Game

A deduction carries its proof with it. When you place a 9 because a 16 crosses a 17, you know why the 9 is there, and that reason holds no matter what happens later. A guess carries no proof. Every digit you place after it depends on it, and if the guess is wrong, all of them are wrong too.

The real cost shows up late. A bad guess rarely fails right away. It fails ten or twenty moves later, in a part of the grid that looks unrelated, and by then you can’t untangle which digits came from logic and which came from the coin flip. Wikipedia’s Kakuro article puts it plainly: brute-force guessing is possible, but understanding the combinations an entry can take is the more efficient approach.

Guessing also misses the point of the puzzle. The setter hid a deduction in that corner. Finding it is the game.

Understanding Parity (Even/Odd Logic)

Basic Parity Rules

Three facts from grade school:

even + even = even
odd  + odd  = even
even + odd  = odd

For a two-cell entry, that means the clue tells you the mix before you know a single digit:

Odd clue  (3, 5, 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, 17)  →  one odd digit + one even digit
Even clue (4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16)     →  both odd, or both even

For longer entries the rule generalizes: the clue is odd exactly when the entry holds an odd number of odd digits. A 6 in three cells is {1, 2, 3}, two odds, so the total is even.

Two of the magic blocks have a parity bonus. A 4 in two cells is {1, 3}, and a 16 is {7, 9}, so every cell in a 4 or a 16 is odd. A 3 {1, 2} and a 17 {8, 9} always have one of each.

Applying Parity to the Grid

Parity becomes useful when it crosses another clue. Say a cell sits in a 16 across, so it’s odd. Its down entry is a 10 in two cells, which could be {1, 9}, {2, 8}, {3, 7}, or {4, 6}. The 10 is even, so its two digits are either both odd or both even. The shared cell is odd, so the partner is odd too. {2, 8} and {4, 6} are gone, and the partner is 1 or 3.

It also works with even cells. If a cell has to be even and sits in an 11 in two cells ({2, 9}, {3, 8}, {4, 7}, {5, 6}), it can only be 2, 4, 6, or 8. Its partner takes the odd half: 9, 7, 5, or 3. That’s half the candidates gone without listing a single combination.

Parity never finds anything a full list of combinations wouldn’t. What it gives you is speed. “Odd clue, two cells, so one of each” is a thought you can have at a glance, which makes it the right tool when you’re staring at a stuck corner and need to see its shape.

Advanced Conflict Resolution

The “Ghost” Duplicate

Sometimes a candidate looks fine against both of its own clues, but placing it forces a digit somewhere else that already exists in that entry. The duplicate isn’t on the board yet. It’s a ghost: it only appears if you follow the consequences.

Hunting ghosts means following a forcing chain: assume one candidate, follow only the moves that assumption forces, and watch for a collision. Three rules keep a chain from turning into a guess:

  1. Every link must be forced. “This cell is 4, so its partner in the 5 must be 1.” If a link has two possible outcomes, stop. You’ve started guessing.
  2. Keep it short. Three or four links is a deduction. Fifteen is a guess in disguise.
  3. Never write the assumption down. Trace it in your head or with your finger. If it collapses, you remove one candidate. If it doesn’t collapse, you’ve learned nothing and the grid is untouched.

A chain that ends in a contradiction proves the starting candidate is wrong, so you can cross it out. A chain that ends peacefully proves nothing, so you can’t place the starting candidate just because nothing broke.

Practical Example: Resolving a Deadly Pattern

Sudoku players know the deadly pattern, or unique rectangle: four cells in a rectangle where two digits could swap places without breaking any rule. Kakuro has the same trap. If a 2×2 block of white cells reads x, y over y, x, you can swap x and y and every across sum and every down sum stays the same. A puzzle with one solution can’t end in that shape.

Here’s a grid with something that looks like one. Clue cells read down\across, so 5\ is a down clue of 5 and \16 is an across clue of 16.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 17\   |  4\   | 13\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |       |       |       |  5\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \4  |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The top falls quickly. The 17 down is {8, 9} and the 4 down is {1, 3}. The 11 across starts with one of each. If it started with 9, its last two cells would need to total 2, which is impossible. So it’s 8, and the remaining 3 is 1 + 2, with the 1 under the 4 down. That fixes the 17 across at 9, 3, and 5. The 13 down then needs 13 − 5 − 2 = 6 at its bottom.

Then the corner stalls. The 4 across is {1, 3}, both odd. The 5 down and the 9 down are odd clues, so each has one odd digit and one even digit. Their bottom cells are odd, so their top cells are even: 5 − {1, 3} gives {4, 2}, and 9 − {1, 3} gives {8, 6}.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 17\   |  4\   | 13\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   3   |   5   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |   8   |   1   |   2   |  5\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |   6   |  2 4  |  6 8  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \4  |  1 3  |  1 3  |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Now look at the two ways to finish. Fill A puts 2, 8 on top and 3, 1 below. Fill B puts 4, 6 on top and 1, 3 below. Check the clues: 2 + 3 = 5 and 4 + 1 = 5, so both fill the 5 down. 8 + 1 = 9 and 6 + 3 = 9, so both fill the 9 down. 2 + 8 = 10 and 4 + 6 = 10, so both give the 16 across the 10 it needs. Everything balances. This is where you’d reach for a coin.

Notice, though, that this isn’t a true deadly pattern. In a real one, the same two digits trade places. Here the bottom row swaps 1 and 3, but the top row changes from {2, 8} to {4, 6}, which is a different set of digits. Different digits means some clue can still tell the two fills apart.

Step 1: Assume one candidate. Take the bottom-left cell and suppose it’s 1.

Step 2: Follow only forced moves.

Assume   bottom-left = 1
  → 5 down:     top-left  = 5 − 1 = 4
  → 4 across:   bottom-right = 3
  → 9 down:     top-right = 9 − 3 = 6
  → 16 across:  6 + 4 + 6 = 16 … with two 6s

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |   6   |   4   |  6!   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \4  |  1?   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Step 3: Spot the contradiction. The sum is right, but the 16 across now holds two 6s. The ghost was the 6 placed at the start of that row back when you solved the top. Nothing in the 2×2 corner pointed at it. It sat one cell outside the pattern.

So the bottom-left cell is not 1. It’s 3, and everything else is forced: 2 above it, 1 beside it, 8 above that. Check the 16 across: 6 + 2 + 8 = 16, no repeats.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 17\   |  4\   | 13\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   3   |   5   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \11 |   8   |   1   |   2   |  5\   |  9\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |   6   |   2   |   8   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|#######|   \4  |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

You never wrote the 1, never wrote the 6, and never erased anything. That’s the difference between a forcing chain and a guess.

There’s also a faster, more controversial route. Some solvers argue straight from uniqueness: “if this corner could be a true swap, the puzzle would have two solutions, so it can’t be.” That reasoning only holds because the setter promised one solution, and purists consider it a shortcut rather than a proof. It’s your call. The chain above works whether or not you trust the setter.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

I lost track of the chain halfway through.

  • Cause: Too many links, or a link that wasn’t actually forced.
  • Fix: Start again from the same cell, saying each link out loud (“4, so 1, so 3, so 6”). If any link has two outcomes, abandon the chain and pick a different starting cell.

My chain ended without a contradiction, so I placed the starting digit.

  • Cause: A peaceful chain proves nothing. It only means that branch didn’t break yet.
  • Fix: Erase it. Then run the chain from the other candidate. If that one collapses, the first candidate is correct, for a real reason this time.

Parity told me a cell was odd, and it turned out even.

  • Cause: You applied the two-cell rule to a longer entry. A 9 in three cells can be {2, 3, 4}, one odd digit, or {1, 3, 5}, three.
  • Fix: For three or more cells, parity only fixes whether the count of odd digits is odd or even, not which cells hold them.

Conclusion

Key takeaways:

  1. A valid Kakuro never requires a guess. When two fills look right, one of them breaks a rule you haven’t checked.
  2. Parity reveals the shape of a stuck corner quickly: odd two-cell clues mean one odd and one even digit, and a 4 or 16 means both odd.
  3. Before committing, look for the downstream duplicate. Ghosts usually sit just outside the cells you’re staring at.
  4. A short forcing chain that ends in a collision is a proof. A long one that ends quietly is a guess.

Next steps: Pick up an expert-level puzzle and make one rule for the whole solve: no digit goes on paper unless you can say why it’s there.

title: Eliminating Guesswork in Kakuro: Parity and Logic

content:
Twenty minutes in, the grid is mostly full. You write the last digit of a long across entry, add it up to check, and come up one short. You check the down entry through that cell. It’s off too. You start tracing backward, cell by cell, and the trail keeps going. Ten minutes later you’re erasing half the board and the paper is starting to pill.

Kakuro doesn’t forgive mistakes. Every white cell belongs to two entries, so one wrong digit bends two sums, which bend four more, and the error spreads quietly until something finally refuses to add up, often far from where it started. Almost every ruined grid traces back to one of a few habits, and every one of them can be fixed.

The Fatal Flaw: Guessing

Why 50/50 Is Never Good Enough

You hit a cell that could be a 3 or a 7. Nothing obvious decides it. You pick the 7 to keep moving. It feels harmless: half the time you’ll be right, and you can always fix it later.

Here’s how that plays out. The 7 shrinks the entry it sits in, so a neighboring cell now looks like it must be 4. That 4 sits in an across 5 over two cells, so its partner has to be 1. That 1 also sits in a down 17 over two cells, which needs an 8 or a 9. One cell now has to be 1 and 8-or-9 at the same time.

The grid broke at that 1, but the error was the 7, two moves earlier, and nothing on the page tells you which digit was the guess. In a real solve, you’d have placed a dozen other digits in between, and every one of them looks just as confident as the rest.

That’s what makes guessing expensive. Kakuro is a tightly connected web of constraints, and a wrong digit doesn’t stay where you put it. When you fix it, you also have to unwind everything it touched.

The better approach: a published Kakuro has one solution, reachable by logic. If you’re tempted to guess, you’ve missed something. Go back and check:

  • Is there an entry with only one or two empty cells left? Subtract and see what’s forced.
  • Have you listed the full combinations for the longest entry through that cell?
  • Did you update pencil marks after your last few placements?

Usually one of those three answers the question you were about to flip a coin on.

The Duplicate Digit Trap

Losing Track of the Entry

Long entries are where duplicates hide. You place a 4 in the first cell of a seven-cell entry early in the solve. Fifteen minutes later you’re working the other end of that same entry, and a 4 fits nicely. The first one is five cells back, and you don’t look that far.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \29 |   4   |   1   |   2   |   3   |   6   |   4   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

Add it up: 4 + 1 + 2 + 3 + 6 + 4 + 9 = 29. The sum checks out. The entry is still illegal, because the 4 appears twice. This is the nasty part of the duplicate trap: your arithmetic check passes, so nothing warns you.

It’s worse than it looks. 29 in seven cells is a unique sum: the only legal set is {1,2,3,4,5,6,8}. There’s no 9 in that set at all. Checking the combination before filling would have caught both errors at once.

Fix it with a full-length scan. Before you write any digit in pen, look left along the entry all the way to its black cell, then right all the way to the next black cell. Then do the same up and down. It takes two seconds, and it catches every duplicate before it can spread.

The Pencil Mark Failure

Not Erasing Eliminated Options

Pencil marks only help if they’re current. You note {3,5,7} in a cell, then place a 5 elsewhere in the same entry. If you don’t erase the 5 from that cell’s marks right away, it stays there looking like a live option. Later, tired and moving quickly, you see a cell down to “two candidates,” pick the 5, and you’ve written a duplicate based on your own outdated notes.

Stale pencil marks are worse than none, because they look like information.

Use the same routine every time you place a digit in pen:

The Pencil Mark Update Flow

Tracking the required updates after placing a digit:

graph TD
    A[Place Final Digit] --> B(Erase from Across Entry)
    A --> C(Erase from Down Entry)
    B --> D[Recalculate Remaining Across Sum]
    C --> E[Recalculate Remaining Down Sum]
    D --> F{Any Singles Left?}
    E --> F
    F -->|Yes| G[New Forced Digit Found]
    F -->|No| H[Continue Solving]
  1. Erase that digit from every pencil mark in the cell’s across entry.
  2. Erase it from every pencil mark in the cell’s down entry.
  3. Recalculate the remaining sum for both entries. A 10 over three cells with a 1 placed is now a 9 over two cells, which can’t use 1.
  4. Look for singles. Any cell in either entry that’s down to one candidate is your next move.

The routine also hands you your next deduction most of the time, so it pays for itself.

The Arithmetic Slip

A lot of broken grids come down to plain addition, not bad logic. You think 8 + 5 is 14, the logic built on top of it is flawless, and the grid falls apart anyway.

Two habits prevent most of it. First, when an entry has one cell left, compute its value as the clue minus the placed digits, then add the full entry back up to confirm. Second, check the crossing entry the same way before you move on. Two independent checks on the same cell rarely fail the same way.

Do’s and Don’ts

Do:

  • ✓ Scan the full length of the across and down entries before writing a digit in pen.
  • ✓ Stop and recalculate when you feel the urge to guess. The urge means you’ve missed something.
  • ✓ Keep unproven digits in pencil. Ink only what you can prove.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Rush long entries of five cells or more. That’s where duplicates hide.
  • ✗ Assume a digit is right because it fits one direction. It has to fit both.
  • ✗ Erase the whole board when a contradiction shows up. Trace back through the cells that fed it and erase only that chain.

If you’re just starting out, practice somewhere that checks your work. KakuroConquest’s free browser puzzles show the possible combinations when you click a clue, and its check button highlights duplicate digits and wrong sums in red. Once your scanning habits are solid, move to paper, where nothing catches you.

Conclusion

Most Kakuro failures aren’t failures of logic. They’re habits that let a small slip spread across the grid. Fix the habits and the logic you already have starts working.

Key takeaways:

  1. Guessing breaks the puzzle. If you’re tempted, you’ve missed a deduction, so go find it.
  2. Check for duplicate digits across the entire entry, from black cell to black cell, every time.
  3. Update pencil marks the moment you place a digit, and erase eliminated options right away.
  4. Confirm every completed entry with a second addition check, in both directions.

Next steps: If you came to Kakuro from Sudoku, some of your instincts will work against you. The next article covers exactly which ones.

content:
You want a Kakuro that opens a padlock. The lock takes three digits, and the plan is simple: solve the grid, read three shaded cells, turn the dials. Then you try it. You fill the grid first, shade three cells that happen to look nice, and read off 3-8-6. The lock was set to 4-0-7 weeks ago. Your grid gave you whatever digits the fill happened to produce, and no Kakuro cell can ever hold a 0 anyway.

The answer has to come first. The grid gets built around it.

A grid that hides an answer is still a Kakuro: it needs one solution, a fair solving path and a clean layout. On top of that, a few cells have to hold digits you chose before you started. This article covers how to read an answer out of a grid, the digit traps that rule some answers out, how to build a grid around fixed digits, and how to control when the answer becomes readable. It uses the same 7x7 layout as the rest of this series.

Reading an Answer Out of a Grid

Mark a few white cells: shading, a heavy border or a small symbol all work. When the grid is solved, the solver reads those cells in a fixed order to get the answer.

State the reading order, or make it obvious. Normal reading order, left to right and top to bottom, is the safest default because nobody needs telling. The answer can be a lock code, a page number to turn to, or a number that feeds the next puzzle.

Here’s the series Main grid from How to Make Sure Your Kakuro Has Exactly One Solution, solved, with three cells shaded: r1c4, r2c4 and r4c3.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 16\   | 12\   | 10\   |  8\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \12 |   6   |   3   |   2   |  [1]  |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \27 |   9   |   6   |   8   |  [4]  | 21\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \3  |   1   |   2   | 19\8  |   3   |   5   |  6\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \8  |   1   |  [7]  | 17\8  |   6   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \16 |   4   |   8   |   3   |   1   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \27 |   8   |   9   |   7   |   3   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

In reading order: 1, 4, 7. That works here because the shaded cells were picked to fit a grid that already existed. For a real lock or a real page, you need the opposite: the digits are fixed, and the grid has to fit them.

The Digit Traps

Some answers can’t come out of a Kakuro at all, and some can only come out of certain cells. Check these before you build anything.

No zeros. Nikoli’s first rule is “Put numbers from 1 through 9 in each cell (No zeros).” So 4-0-7, page 105 or the year 2010 can’t be read straight off the grid. Either choose answers without a 0, or use a conversion like “add the shaded cells together,” which can produce a zero-containing total.

Repeated digits need separate runs. No digit repeats within a run. If your answer is 4-7-4, the two cells holding 4 can’t sit in the same across run or the same down run. In the Main grid above, r1c4 and r2c4 share a down run, which is fine for 1 and 4 but rules out a code like 4-4-7 for those two cells.

Some digits barely fit some runs. A cell in a 4-cell run with a clue of 10 can only hold 1, 2, 3 or 4, because 10 in four cells is {1, 2, 3, 4}. If your answer needs a 9 there, that clue is off the table.

Building the Grid Around the Answer

Step by Step

You’re building a grid on the series layout that hides the code 4-7-4.

1. Pick the answer cells. The two 4s need separate runs, and spreading the cells out keeps the answer from clustering in one corner. Use r2c2, r4c5 and r5c3. Each sits in a different across run and a different down run, and they read in that order left to right, top to bottom.

2. Lock the digits. Write 4 in r2c2, 7 in r4c5 and 4 in r5c3. From here on, those three cells don’t change, whatever else does.

3. Fill around them. Write digits in the other 21 white cells with no repeats in any run, then add up all 16 clues. This is the same fill-first step from the rest of the series, with three cells already decided.

4. Repair without touching the locked cells. The first fill will almost certainly have more than one solution. Change one unlocked digit at a time and keep each change if the number of solutions doesn’t go up, until only one is left. If a swap involves a locked cell, the repair has to break it using the other corners.

5. Check the grade, not just the count. One solution isn’t enough. The grid also has to be solvable by logic.

With the solve-order check from later in this article added, the full loop looks like this:

Doing It with the Series Code

The solver from Build a Kakuro Solver and Generator in Python handles steps 3–5. Its random_fill takes a fixed set of cells, and repair takes a locked set it won’t change:

"""hidden.py: build a grid around a fixed answer, then check it."""
import random
import sys

from kakuro import grade, random_fill, read_grid, repair, with_totals
from generate import to_text

ANSWER = {(2, 2): 4, (4, 5): 7, (5, 3): 4}   # code 4-7-4, read in reading order

with open("layout.txt", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    layout = f.read()
cells, runs = read_grid(layout)
rng = random.Random(int(sys.argv[1]) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else 1)

for attempt in range(1, 11):
    fill = random_fill(cells, runs, rng, fixed=ANSWER)
    if repair(cells, runs, fill, rng, locked=ANSWER):
        puzzle = to_text(layout, with_totals(runs, fill))
        code = "-".join(str(fill[x]) for x in sorted(ANSWER))
        print(f"unique after attempt {attempt}, code {code}\n{puzzle}\ngrade: {grade(puzzle)}")
        break
else:
    print("no unique grid in 10 attempts; try another seed or move the answer cells")

Put it next to kakuro.py, generate.py and layout.txt from that article. The first run, python hidden.py 1, produced a grid with exactly one solution and this grade:

grade: Expert or guessing: needs parity, chains, or search (Tier 4+)

That’s step 5 earning its place. A unique grid can still be one the solver can’t finish without guessing, and a hidden-answer grid that needs a guess is worse than useless: the solver will guess, get the code wrong and blame the lock. Throw it out. Across seeds 1 through 7, four grids graded Easy/Medium, one graded Hard, and two needed Tier 4 or guessing. Every one had exactly one solution, and every one still read 4-7-4. Seed 2 gave this:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 18\   | 16\   |  8\   |  9\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \15 |       |       |       |       |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |       |  []   |       |       | 22\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |       |       |  8\7  |       |       | 16\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \4  |       |       |  6\12 |  []   |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \26 |  []   |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \12 |       |       |       |       |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

One solution, solvable with magic blocks and intersections, three of them in the clues: 10 across in row 2 ({1, 2, 3, 4}), 17 across in row 3 ({8, 9}) and 4 across in row 4 ({1, 3}). Solved:

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######| 18\   | 16\   |  8\   |  9\   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \15 |   7   |   1   |   5   |   2   |#######|#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \10 |   2   |  [4]  |   3   |   1   | 22\   |#######|
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \17 |   9   |   8   |  8\7  |   6   |   1   | 16\   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|   \4  |   3   |   1   |  6\12 |  [7]  |   5   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \26 |  [4]  |   5   |   8   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|#######|#######|   \12 |   3   |   1   |   6   |   2   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

4, 7, 4. The lock opens.

If you’re building by hand instead, the steps are the same. Write the three locked digits in ink, fill the rest in pencil, and repair with the swap checks from the uniqueness article, never touching the ink.

When the Answer Appears

The order in which cells get solved matters more in a hidden-answer grid than anywhere else. If the solver can read the whole code after a handful of moves, they’ll try the lock and skip the rest of your puzzle.

Look at the 4-7-4 grid. r2c2 sits inside the 10 across in row 2, a magic block, and it’s one of the first cells to fall. The solver has the first 4 almost immediately. That’s fine on its own, because the other two digits hold out. In a straightforward solve, r4c5, the 7, is the 21st of 24 cells placed. The full code isn’t readable until the grid is nearly done.

The Main grid’s 1-4-7 behaves the same way. r1c4 and r2c4 fall around the middle of the solve, and r4c3 is one of the last few cells placed.

To check your own grid, solve it from blank and number the cells as you fill them. Then look at where the answer cells land:

  • At least one answer cell should fall late. That’s what keeps the solver solving.
  • Not every answer cell should sit in a magic block. A magic block hands its digits over at the start.
  • If the whole answer arrives early, move an answer cell. Pick one that falls late in your numbered solve, then lock and repair again.

Wrong Answers

A one-digit mistake in the grid usually shows up as a broken sum somewhere else, and the solver goes back and finds it. But sometimes a slip only affects a shaded cell, and the solver walks away with a wrong answer that looks fine.

For a lock, that’s self-correcting: the lock doesn’t open, and the solver rechecks. For a page number it’s riskier, because a wrong page might happen to continue the story. If 147 is the answer, a single wrong digit gives 117, 127, 137, 157, 141–146, 148 or 149. A book that uses page-number answers needs each of those to say clearly that the solver slipped. That’s book design more than grid design, but it starts with knowing which wrong answers your shaded cells can produce.

Case Study: Escape the Crimson Gala

Escape the Crimson Gala is a murder-mystery escape-room book where every door opens with a Kakuro grid. You’re a rookie officer locked inside the Stanton tower with 400 donors and a killer, and each grid is the next door. According to the book’s description:

  • Shaded squares give the page number. Read them in order and turn to that page. Nobody can flip ahead, because nobody knows where the story goes next until they’ve solved the grid.
  • A wrong sum lands on a dead end, which tells the solver at once that they slipped and shows them how to find the mistake.
  • Ten training grids come first, for readers who’ve never solved a Kakuro.
  • All 50 puzzles have exactly one answer reachable by logic.

Each choice maps to a grid-design problem from this series. Page-number answers are hidden answers with the stakes turned up, so every one has to clear the digit traps above. The dead ends handle wrong answers. The training grids are the difficulty ramp from How to Set Kakuro Difficulty: easy grids teach the puzzle before it guards anything important. And “one answer reachable by logic” is the standard every grid in this series is built to.

A Checklist for Hidden-Answer Grids

Run this on every grid before anyone else sees it:

  1. The answer has no 0, or there’s a conversion rule that handles it.
  2. Repeated answer digits sit in separate runs.
  3. The answer cells were locked before the fill, and nothing changed them afterward.
  4. The grid has exactly one solution.
  5. The grid solves by logic, with no guessing (Tier 3 at most, unless you mean to go further).
  6. At least one answer cell falls late in a numbered solve.
  7. The solved grid reads the right answer in the stated order.

Repeat 3–7 after any change to the grid, even one that has nothing to do with the answer cells. A repair elsewhere can change the solve order, or the grade.

Best Practices

Do:

  • ✓ Choose the answer before you build the grid.
  • ✓ Lock the answer cells and repair around them.
  • ✓ Check the grade as well as the solution count.
  • ✓ Number a test solve to see when the answer becomes readable.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Shade cells after the fill and hope the digits work out.
  • ✗ Put two identical answer digits in the same run.
  • ✗ Put every answer cell inside a magic block.

Troubleshooting

The repair never reaches one solution. The locked cells sit on a swap that can only be broken by changing them. Move one answer cell to a different spot (keeping repeated digits in separate runs), lock again and repeat. Answer cells inside 2x2 white blocks are the likeliest culprits, since that’s where swaps live.

The answer is readable after a few moves. Every answer cell falls early, often because each one sits in a magic block or crosses one. Move one answer cell somewhere that falls late in your numbered solve.

The answer changed after a fix. A repair touched an answer cell, usually because it wasn’t locked. Re-lock the answer, restore its digits and repair again.

The grid is unique but solvers get stuck. It needs Tier 4 deductions or a guess. Check the grade; if it’s past what you intended, try another fill around the same locked cells.

Putting It Together

A hidden answer is a constraint you set before the grid exists. Check it against the digit traps: no zeros, and repeated digits in separate runs. Lock the answer cells, fill around them, and repair without touching them. Then check two things beyond the solution count: that the grid solves by logic, and that the answer arrives late enough to keep the solver solving.

Pick a three-digit code with no zeros and build it into the series layout, by hand or with hidden.py. To see hidden answers working across a whole book, Escape the Crimson Gala has 50 grids, and every door opens with one.

content:
You can finish a hard Sudoku in ten minutes. You spot X-wings without trying, and naked pairs jump out at you. So you flip to the Kakuro page expecting a warm-up, and twenty minutes later you’ve placed four digits, erased three of them, and you’re refusing to write a 5 in a cell because there’s already a 5 further along the row.

That 5 is legal, by the way. You aren’t bad at Kakuro. You’re running Sudoku instincts on a puzzle that only looks similar. Both use the digits 1 through 9, both ban repeats, and both are solved with pencil marks and pure deduction. But the rules underneath work differently, and a few of your best Sudoku habits will steer you wrong.

What Stays the Same

The Logic-First Mindset

The most important skill carries over intact: you never guess. A well-made Kakuro has exactly one solution, and every digit can be proven, the same as a well-made Sudoku. The discipline you built, refusing to place a digit until you’ve earned it, is the most valuable thing you bring.

Your notation carries over too. Pencil marks (candidates) work exactly the same way: small digits in the corner of a cell, erased as they’re ruled out. If you already have a tidy candidate system, keep it.

And the digit range is the same: 1 through 9, no zeros. That’s where the overlap ends.

The Major Differences

Math Replaces the 3x3 Box

Sudoku has no arithmetic. The digits are just nine distinct symbols. You could replace them with nine colors or nine letters and every technique would still work. A 9 isn’t bigger than a 1. It’s just different.

In Kakuro, the digits are quantities. Every clue is a sum, and every deduction starts with “which digits can add up to this?” A 9 is worth nine 1s, and that changes how you think. Sudoku logic is spatial: where in this row can the 7 go? Kakuro logic is combinational: which sets of digits make 23 in three cells, and which of those fit here?

The grid is different too. Sudoku is always a 9x9 square with 81 cells and nine 3x3 boxes. Kakuro grids look like crosswords, come in many sizes, and have no boxes. Each constraint is a straight line of white cells between two black cells, and entries can be anywhere from two to nine cells long.

The Scope of the “No Duplicate” Rule

This is the one that trips up Sudoku players most.

  • Sudoku: no repeated digit in any row, column, or 3x3 box.
  • Kakuro: no repeated digit within a single entry. That’s all.

A Kakuro row can contain several separate entries, split by black cells. Each one is its own small problem with its own clue. The same digit can appear in every one of them.

+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+
|   \8  |   5   |   3   |   \14 |   5   |   9   |
+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+-------+

The Boundary Logic

Why duplicates are legal across black cells:

graph TD
    A[Row] --> B[Black Cell Clue 8]
    A --> C[Black Cell Clue 14]
    B --> D[Entry 1: 5 + 3]
    C --> E[Entry 2: 5 + 9]
    D -.->|Isolated| E
    style D fill:#2d2d2d,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff
    style E fill:#2d2d2d,stroke:#fff,stroke-width:2px,color:#fff

Two 5s in the same row, just like the one you refused to write. In Sudoku, that’s an immediate error. Here it’s perfectly legal. The first 5 belongs to the across 8 (5 + 3), and the second belongs to the across 14 (5 + 9). The black cell between them ends one entry and starts a new one.

Treat every entry as its own small world. Once a black cell ends an entry, forget everything to the right of it.

Adapting Your Techniques

Naked Pairs to Unique Sums

Your Sudoku pattern-spotting doesn’t go to waste. Most techniques have a Kakuro counterpart, and some of them get easier.

Take naked pairs. In Sudoku, you work to discover that two cells in a unit can only hold {1,2}, and then you eliminate 1 and 2 from the rest of that unit. In Kakuro, a clue of 3 over two cells hands you that same {1,2} lock immediately, because 1 + 2 is the only way to make 3. These clues are called unique sums, and they’re your starting points.

The full naked-pair technique still works inside long Kakuro entries, too. If two cells in a six-cell entry are both locked to {8,9} by their crossing clues, no other cell in that entry can be an 8 or a 9.

Here’s how the rest of your toolkit translates:

Sudoku habit Kakuro equivalent
Starting from the given digits Starting from unique sums: 3, 4, 16, and 17 in two cells
Scanning a row for its missing digit Scanning entries for clues with only one combination
Naked pair locked to {1,2} A 3 over two cells, which is {1,2} by arithmetic
Crossing row and column candidates Cross-referencing a cell’s across and down entries
A row with one empty cell left An entry with one empty cell: clue minus placed digits
No repeats in row, column, box No repeats within a single entry

That first row is worth repeating. Kakuro has no givens. The unique sums are your givens. You just have to recognize them.

If you want a gentler bridge, try Killer Sudoku. It uses a standard Sudoku grid, but its cells are grouped into dotted-line cages of two to nine cells, each marked with a sum, and digits can’t repeat within a cage. You get to practice the arithmetic side of Kakuro while the Sudoku rules you already know keep you on track.

Do’s and Don’ts

Do:

  • ✓ Embrace the math. Memorize the common combinations the way you once memorized Sudoku patterns.
  • ✓ Use your Sudoku scanning speed for cross-referencing. Checking an across entry against a down entry is a skill you already have.
  • ✓ Keep your candidate notation exactly as it is.

Don’t:

  • ✗ Scan a whole row from edge to edge looking for a missing digit. Look only at the entry between its black cells.
  • ✗ Refuse a digit because it already appears elsewhere in the row. If a black cell separates them, it’s legal.

Troubleshooting Common Issues

“I keep refusing to place digits that are actually legal.” That’s Sudoku muscle memory. Before you rule out a digit for repeating, find the black cells at both ends of the entry and check only between them. After a few grids, the new boundary will feel natural.

“I can’t find anywhere to start. There are no given digits.” Kakuro gives you sums instead. Scan for clues near the extremes of what their entry can hold: 3 or 4 over two cells, 16 or 17 over two cells, 6 or 24 over three cells. Each one tells you its digits outright.

“I know the digits but can’t figure out the order.” Sudoku taught you to cross row candidates with column candidates. Do the same thing here with the across and down entries through the cell. The digit has to appear in both lists.

Conclusion

You already have the hardest skill Kakuro asks for: the patience to prove every digit before you write it. What changes is where your evidence comes from. In Sudoku it comes from position. In Kakuro it comes from addition.

Key takeaways:

  1. Kakuro requires addition. Sudoku doesn’t, and that changes how you start and how you deduce.
  2. The no-duplicate rule applies only within a single entry, not across a whole row or column.
  3. Your pencil marks, your scanning speed, and your refusal to guess are your biggest assets.
